Utilizing the multivariate method and resultant elimination techniques, we establish novel categories of sparse permutation polynomials over finite fields with cube orders, with various degrees of completeness, for any $q=p^{k}$ where the prime $p$ exceeds $2$.

Approximately $4$ billion individuals worldwide are affected by intestinal
parasites. The health risks associated with these infections cause a multitude
of issues, such as physical and mental disorders, often resulting in the death
of young children and immunocompromised individuals. Notwithstanding a propensity
for human diagnostic error, visual inspection is still predominantly utilized
for clinical diagnoses. Previous studies exploring the application of computer-
aided intestinal parasite classification have faced challenges due to the visual
similarities between parasites and other contaminants in fecal matter. This
paper introduces Deep Belief Networks as a solution to the challenges of
automatic intestinal parasite classification, presenting successful results from
three comprehensive datasets featuring images of eggs, larvae, and protozoa,
despite including scenarios with uneven distribution of classes and contaminants.

This work introduces a novel approximation technique for a broad category of zero-sum-free stochastic differential investment and reinsurance models. It incorporates both proportional reinsurance and loss-overlimit reinsurance models. To calculate the Nash equilibrium, a Markov chain approximation approach and a dynamical programming technique are used to solve nonlinear integro-differential Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equations. In addition, the research shows the convergence of the approximating sequences to the accurate solution of the value functions, which is supported by several numerical case studies.

This research presents a novel Proportional-Integral-Derivative-Accelerated (PIDA) control strategy, integrating a derivative filter, to enhance quadcopter stability in chaotic and unpredictable flight conditions. The mathematical framework is established based on a highly accurate model that effectively accounts for non-linearities, uncertainty, and interdependence. The integration of measurement noise and uncertainty can lead to flight instability, and our proposed controller paired with a heuristic Genetic Filter (GF) successfully tackles these challenges. The PIDA controller is tuned via Stochastic Dual (SD) optimization, leveraging its performance and reliability. The combined PIDA and GF algorithms exhibit robustness and efficiency in quadcopter flight control, and our simulation results demonstrate the efficacy of our control strategy under various external disturbances and parameter uncertainties.

A comprehensive examination of pion-nucleon interactions at low energy is provided,
with the intention of offering a fundamental and educational overview relevant to current
research endeavors. Key topics addressed include the application of chiral effective
field theory, the significance of the sigma term, an understanding of the qualitative nature
of low-energy phase shifts, the physics governing the $\Delta$ resonance, and isospin violation.
It is emphasized that pion-nucleon scattering at low energy is intrinsically connected to QCD through effective
field theory. Moreover, the need for a more detailed low-energy data set concerning the pion-nucleon sigma term
and isospin violation is underscored in order to meet contemporary research requirements.

The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) is one of the primary detectors in the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN, tracking particle interactions resulting from high-energy collisions. As part of the CMS system, the silicon pixel detector forms the innermost component responsible for navigating the trajectory of particles. Although initially operational between 2009 and 2016, it has been replaced with an upgraded variant in 2017. During a preceding period of shutdown for the LHC, an upgraded forward pixel detector prototype featuring a novel readout system and third disk was introduced, integrating eight pilot blades built using advanced digital readout chips. Through pilot module testing, researchers obtained data, evaluating its efficiency, accuracy, and overall performance. This study aims to document the results of this evaluation, encompassing single-hit resolution, hit efficiency, track-hit and track resolution, and global 4D reconstruction performance.

We have developed a machine learning-based system to identify the types of Active Galactic Nucleus (AGN) host galaxies within the first billion years of the universe's existence. To do this, we employed two AI algorithms. Firstly, we used a transfer learning approach with a pre-trained Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to automatically classify the morphologies of host galaxies into elliptical, spiral, and irregular shapes. Secondly, we trained a Random Forest classifier to combine existing observational data and merge information regarding the host galaxy's appearance with its observed characteristics, such as star formation activity and activity levels. We tested our system with newly collected images of approximately five thousand host galaxies hosting AGNs at redshifts between six and eight. Our findings show that the host galaxies with irregular shapes have greater activity levels than those with spiral or elliptical structures. Furthermore, we discovered that the majority of spiral and elliptical host galaxies are hosting less-luminous AGNs, whereas the irregular hosts often generate more luminous emission. Notably, the host galaxies with lower star formation activity primarily exhibit irregular shapes. To verify these results, we analyzed the specifications of our imaging data using three models based on the characteristics of galaxy disk thickness, star formation activity, and angular separation between the galaxy's disk and the AGN. Our findings indicate that the host galaxies with spiral or elliptical shapes often have distinct separations between the galaxy's disk and the AGN, whereas the irregular hosts may have larger separations or overlapping

High-energy and high-momentum fluctuations occur within the nucleus due to short-range correlations. In order to understand how these correlations affect the nucleus's bulk properties, it's necessary to study their spatial distribution, which will help clarify their relationship between the coordinate and momentum spaces. Employing the lowest-order correlation operator approximation, the distribution of short-range correlations in the nucleus is analyzed through two-dimensional nuclear Wigner phase-space diagrams. This is done by quantifying the asymptotic behavior of the nucleus's phase-space density distribution from its ground state, using $^{16}$O as a reference to examine the impact of short-range correlations on the nucleus's kinetic, potential, and total energy. Additionally, the study reveals that the average prolate-deformation contribution arising from short-range correlations not only modifies the nucleus's collective properties but also significantly impacts its phase-space density distribution.

We are studying complex scaling as an inherent property unique to complex number systems and its applications. By extending the complex domain without considering complex scaling, Deep Complex Networks (DCN) is limited, whereas SurReal achieves scaling invariance but discards complex information. In contrast, we approach complex scaling as a distinct co-domain transformation and create neural network functions tailored for this unique operation. Furthermore, we propose innovative complex-valued representations of RGB images where scaling indicates distinct object identities, thereby enhancing neural network features. By integrating complex scaling, we develop deeper networks while maintaining or reducing parameters, leading to improved performance in various computer vision tasks, including image classification, segmentation, and object detection.

The non-linear QCD evolution equations ultimately lead to the saturation of gluon distribution.  When gluon distribution becomes saturated, it establishes a distinct gluon density threshold per unit rapidity per transverse area known as the saturation momentum.  In certain large-energy situations within specified kinematic domains, saturation momentum becomes the only determining factor in physical processes. Consequently, a variety of observable outcomes display characteristic patterns of geometrical scaling. Several illustrations of such scaling patterns can be seen in various reactions.

A thorough study measured the abundance of twelve key metal elements within eighty-six extremely metal-poor stars residing close to the Sun, focusing on their chemical compositions derived from the analysis of high-resolution spectral data captured using the Large Binocular Telescope and its accompanying equipment. Through an examination of photon-noise, we precisely quantify the inherent abundance variations present among these elements, revealing significant intrinsic scatter across a spectrum ranging from approximately 0.04 dex (in chromium abundance) to 0.16 dex (in sodium abundance) at the sample's average metallicity level. We explored the various factors potentially contributing to these abundance variations and found a suitable explanation for the measured data through the concept of stochastic sampling in the core-collapse supernovae mass distribution, assuming approximately fifty contributing supernovae for the formation of the sample stars at the given metallicity level. Based on this assumption, we deduced that the underlying SN population exhibits relatively low levels of diversity, likely stemming from local and global convective mixing that is capable of covering up the more substantial abundance differences arising from at least ten or more supernovae in the star's formation process.

A novel machine learning approach has been developed that identifies and measures the potential impact of omitted significant predictors on predictive models. The algorithm extends the capabilities of machine learning models to assess their limitations using a new data analysis method based on an observation from a classic study. The method involves comparing an model's original and modified performances with and without a randomly selected subset of predictors. The performance of this algorithm was tested using simulated datasets from two scenarios and real-world datasets from three fields. The results show that while simple machine learning models generally produce optimal results using complete datasets, they often fall short when predicting from a subset of variables. The method was found to effectively evaluate model performance and estimate the potential improvement needed to predict from a reduced set of variables.

Recently, hybrid Quantum-Classical algorithms have shown potential in solving
complex classification issues more effectively than conventional classical methods.
However, their practical application is limited by their dependence on the presence of
a Saddle Point, which makes the Saddle Point Finding problem necessary for these
algorithms to function. This problem can be viewed as a minimax optimization task, 
where the quality of the solution relies heavily on the choice of the objective
function's Saddle Point. Most current approaches use a Saddle Point approximation 
with a focus on minimizing the loss function of a neural network. This work 
approaches the task from a different angle by utilizing reinforcement learning to
define the optimal Saddle Point for the Saddle Point Finding problem. 
Experimental outcomes are presented to demonstrate that utilizing Saddle Points
derived through reinforcement learning leads to better performance on various 
classification issues compared to other existing algorithms.

Researchers, Chen and Garay, have examined pointwise slant submanifolds in almost Hermitian manifolds. By extending the concept of slant submanifolds to semi-slant ones, this study delves into their geometry in both Sasakian and cosymplectic manifolds. Key findings indicate a limitation on semi-slant warped products in Sasakian manifolds. On the other hand, non-trivial semi-slant warped products have been discovered in cosymplectic manifolds, and several foundational results have been obtained, including a defining characteristic of such semi-slant warped products.

The PALEOCCENE concept has the potential to develop sensitive and efficient low-energy detectors that can operate at room temperature and are minimally maintained. Such detectors could range in weight from grams to kilograms and could detect nuclear recoil events triggered by various factors including neutron scattering, CEvNS, or interactions with dark matter. Ongoing research, including existing and planned studies, is being conducted to explore the practicality of this technique for multiple applications.

We examine a rigid structure composed of two active Brownian particles that interact in an activity gradient. We demonstrate analytically that the dimer exhibits either tandem or side-walking behavior, contingent upon the alignment of its direction of motion and the gradient vector. Furthermore, we find that tandem and side-walking dynamics coexist through the dimer's internal rotation, and also result in the dimer moving in parallel or perpendicularly to the gradient in the absence of a specific alignment mechanism. If such an alignment mechanism exists, the dimer's components effectively 'take a short cut' round the gradient, thereby facilitating faster movement compared to its side-walking state. We discuss theoretical and experimental side-walking scenarios, including those involving confined environments. This research may inspire the design of novel active colloidal materials with unique properties.

We investigate numerically charge-neutral collective excitations in fractional quantum Hall systems, focusing on two specific Jain states, ν=2/7 and ν=2/9 near quarter filling, and the 1/4 Fermi-liquid state, contrasting them with the behavior observed in 1/3 states and those near half filling. Unlike those latter states, ν=2/7 and ν=2/9 each display magnetoroton spectral densities with two peaks rather than one, featuring magnetorotons with a spin of 2, whose chiralities differ for the 2/7 and 2/9 states, but share the same chirality in the 2/9 case. Our calculations also affirm the theoretical prediction that connects the emergence of a certain type of excitations to the minimal spin value of magnetorrtons, specifically showing that ν=2/9 exhibits the expected type of excitations while data for the 2/7 state suggests it may only partially satisfy this criterion.

Epidemics on massive contact networks with millions of individuals pose significant challenges for analysis and containment due to their immense scale. However, forking algorithms can significantly reduce the computational burden by leveraging graph structure to pinpoint key areas requiring analysis, enabling researchers to study the required level of detail. By dividing the network into micro-groups for each outbreak to occur, researchers can analyze the spread within each cluster isolation. This novel approach, inspired by the'slice and dice' method, incorporates various algorithms to break down the network and link them to statistical methods to study the spread. This fully automated system allows the creation of realistic outbreak scenarios to test response strategies to real-time epidemics without the need for manual intervention.

The maximum likelihood estimator used in CMB map-making provides optimal, unbiased results as long as the underlying data model is accurate, but inaccuracies often arise due to sub-pixel structures, instrumentation flaws such as time-varying gain and pointing errors, leading to model inaccuracy in practice. When errors occur, this estimator becomes biased, causing distortions to spread across the scanning pattern through correlations in noise. A notable effect of this phenomenon is the creation of 'X'-shaped patterns surrounding strong point sources in typical satellite scanning patterns. This paper examines why such distortion occurs and introduces both established and novel techniques for mitigating its effects, including accompanying scanning parameters, data monte carlo methods, fourier deconvolution, and multi-frequency analysis. Although the specific types and severity of errors can vary depending on the satellite and scanning strategy used, the X-shape caused by point sources remains a notable feature of all major CMB map-making data sets, highlighting the need for adequate correction methods.

Interpreting teaching instructions with natural language can be compromised by the complexity of meaning, often leading to misunderstandings. Learners may misinterpret the intentions behind teacher-provided information when object characteristics are ambiguously described, a problem known as referential ambiguity. We explore how principles from cognitive sciences, such as teaching strategies (tailoring instructions) and adapting to agent preferences, can mitigate referential ambiguities through induction. Our experiments involve training algorithms to accomplish tasks described using uncertain common sense knowledge, and our results suggest that incorporating these ideas enhances the ability to disambiguate object characteristics under uncertain conditions.

Quantum process tomography is crucial for building quantum computers, establishing quantum networks, and developing quantum sensors. Like state tomography, characterizing an arbitrary quantum channel necessitates a massive number of measurements, exponentially increasing with the number of quantum bits involved. Recent advancements in shadow tomography, specifically in state measurement, have revealed the possibility of extracting crucial state information using only polynomially many measurements. This study brings the concepts of shadow state tomography to the forefront, addressing the challenge of quantum process characterization. We introduce process shadow tomography, focusing on two primary scenarios: reconstructing arbitrary quantum channels and deriving a universal channel estimation error bound for any n-qubit channel. Furthermore, the research demonstrates the applicability of process shadow tomography to noisy channels, showcasing its potential in analyzing real-world channels with limited resources. Future developments could involve the adaptation of process shadow tomography from quantum to classical channels, offering a more efficient measurement scheme compared to traditional quantum channel estimation techniques.

We aim to derive precise bounds for the Cheeger constant using a range of geometric attributes such as area, perimeter, inradius, circumradius, minimum width and diameter. Our approach involves establishing tight inequalities among these measures specifically for planar convex bodies, along with formulating new conjectures that stem from numerical experiments.

The advent of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) holds great potential for transforming communications systems. By harnessing their adaptability and swift deployment capabilities, it becomes feasible to supply content in densely populated areas or regions lacking essential infrastructure. In this study, we explore a UAV model that serves a maximum number of users at various locations within a set time frame. To achieve optimal trajectory planning, we develop a mixed-integer linear program for problem formulation. For large-scale problems involving a staggering number of trajectory options, we establish a link to the orienteering problem, subsequently proposing an efficient greedy algorithm. Simulation results validate the efficacy and rapidity of this proposed algorithm, yielding solutions comparable to the optimal outcomes. Consequently, this approach can be utilized for planning strategic content caching and tactical field operations.

The low-energy electronic structure of an unbiased bilayer graphene, characterized by quadratic dispersions at two Fermi points when high-order contributions are disregarded, differs qualitatively from that of single-layer graphene. We found that this difference becomes similar to that of single-layer graphene when the short-range interactions are taken into account in a specific context. Specifically, this happens when the short-range interactions' momentum-space projections are confined to a narrow angular range, like $O(1/N)$, where $N$ represents the number of valleys in the system, indicating a breakdown of Wigner-Douglas symmetry. Consequently, this leads to the short-range interactions causing a non-uniform screening effect, substituting the short-range interactions' momentum-space projections with a unangular $O(1)$ value and making low-energy electronic structure robust against variations in the short-range interactions. Under these conditions, we found that effective short-range anisotropy-induced velocity renormalizations establish a similarity between bilayer graphene and single-layer graphene. Furthermore, this study also highlights the role of the door.

The conformation of surface molecules can greatly affect the interaction between a sample and a scanner in molecular-based devices. For these devices to be integrated into broader technological platforms, it is vital to understand how to manipulate the conformation of these molecules. The interaction between a scanner and a device's surface is typically modeled as an interaction between an object (the scanner) and an infinitesimally small point (the sample), however in the context of molecular devices this model falls short as molecular interactions are predominantly based on shape. Using Sc2TbN@C80 on a gold surface we demonstrate that temperature induced changes in metal magnetic moment leads to corresponding changes in work function and electron transport. The conformation of these molecules interacts strongly with the underlying gold surface however through thermal energy the interaction transforms into a loose bound state resulting in a notable increase in work function and scanner-surface interaction strength. The conformation of these molecules falls within an expected range however this change in interaction can be utilized for highly sensitive detection of molecular shape changes which could serve as a building block for future molecular-based devices, and it provides a model system for studying the conformation of surface molecules.

The internet of things encompasses a network of interconnected devices, which includes various non-standard gadgets, traditionally unlinked to the internet, at an exponentially growing pace. Data security and user privacy concerns loom large over the IoT landscape, where devices operate on low power. Conventional encryption methods are unsuitable for these devices, necessitating a need for contemporary lightweight algorithms tailored for IoT settings, which this communication seeks to summarize.

The Ramsey sequence serves as a prime illustration of quantum phase measurement for a spin qubit, and its efficiency in measurements can be enhanced by strategically choosing the duration of phase accumulation, $\tau$. A sequential Bayesian experimental approach is employed to determine the length of the Ramsey sequence that minimizes the uncertainty of the measured phase in the presence of spin qubit relaxation. When the qubit relaxation process is characterized as a first-order Markov chain, simulations reveal that the Bayesian method yields results approximately 40% better than an earlier random measurement strategy. Moreover, when the relaxation corresponds to an exponential decay, the computational efficiency of the Bayesian approach is greatly improved, allowing it to be run in real-time throughout the experiment, and it is found that its performance is within 93% of the optimal results.

Gromov centrality pinpoints key nodes in networks by measuring the deviation from the standard triangle inequality, where core nodes sit at the perimeter of a circle with an excess close to 1, in contrast to the core of the network, which is closer to the origin. A mathematical investigation into this concept reveals its application extends beyond spatial networks to more general metric spaces. Furthermore, its practical utility is demonstrated through its successful identification of critical components in various real-world networks, such as air transportation systems, as well as its use in visualizing the metric structure of these networks.

From a purely non-relativistic perspective, we derive the Poisson equation solution for empty space in a scenario with a rotating gravitational system, analogous to the Sun, and consider the implications of this solution for the behavior of test objects within its gravitational field. The general solution to the Poisson equation, expressed in terms of the distance r and angle θ, is shown to exhibit properties consistent with Newton's inverse square law of gravitation to the lowest order approximation. This analysis yields two significant outcomes when considered up to the second-order approximation: firstly, the observed perihelion shift of the solar planets, and secondly, an explanation for the precession of the solar planets' axes, which correlates with Einstein's century-old theory of general relativity, although this analysis does so in a non-relativistic manner, attributing the outcomes to the azimuthally symmetric gravitational field generated by the spinning Sun, and demonstrating that these effects are evident within a non-relativistic framework, and may be understandable without invoking the principles of special or general relativity.

Sets of matrix pencils sharing the same Kronecker canonical form are classified under strict equivalence into infinite groups called bundles. Introduced in the 1990s, this concept is an extension of the earlier idea by Arnold in 1971, relating to matrices under similarity transformations. Despite substantial research on the topology of bundles of matrix pencils, key questions remain unanswered for linear connections, projective bundles, and matrix bundles. Our innovations include introducing a novel metric on the space of flags for matrix pencils and developing a linear connection on the space of pencils of quadratic forms. Additionally, we use the flag metric and linear connection to distinguish bundles of symmetric matrix pencils.

The $C^*$-algebra formalism of topological T-duality developed by Mathai and Rosenberg is applied to a broad class of topological spaces encompassing torus bundles, nilmanifolds, and other examples. By constructing T-duals from commutative $C^*$-algebras with one connected component, we demonstrate almost Abelian solvmanifolds have a unique T-dual. Our method also reveals the pivotal role of stochastic matrices in achieving T-duals of torus bundles, showcasing both analytical and cohomological approaches. Furthermore, the monodromy matrices obtained through stochastic matrices are distinct from those obtained through periodic functions, except in the trivial case. Eventually, the construction of T-duals for Ray classified almost Abelian solvmanifolds enables the determination of T-duals for certain K3 surfaces, an outcome independent of the $C^*$-algebra approach.

Cohen-Addad, Filtser, Klein, and Le started an investigation into whether sparse graphs can be efficiently represented using short node labels. Unfortunately, it was found that minor-free graphs with a certain bound on treewidth require at least O(n) labels on some nodes, despite expectations of a better outcome. In response to this challenge, we have developed a new method for embedding these graphs into lattices. As a result, we obtain a new lower bound for the treewidth of minor-free graphs with O(n) nodes, which aligns with an existing theorem by Baker. Moreover, our approach leads to improved approximate algorithms for graph partitioning, which is a significant result in its own right. In detail, our embeddings provide the basis for a new algorithm capable of finding an O(log n)-approximation for the tree decomposition of minor-free graphs within O(n) time, significantly surpassing previous results for an O(n log n) approximation in the same setting. Additionally, our technique extends to the analysis of sparse graphs with a constant minimum degree, where we derive bounds on the treewidth, chordal width, and maximum clique number of such graphs, all of which remain uncertain until now.

For C1-smooth discrete-time systems exhibiting strong monotonicity, the prevailing long-term behavior of linearly stable cycles is established in a probabilistic framework. This research then extends to periodic parabolic equations and reveals new findings regarding the ubiquity of periodic solution convergence. Notably, in Neumann-bound equations defined on convex domains, the set of initial conditions corresponding to homogeneous periodic solutions is shown to be prevalent, while in radially symmetric domains, the set of radially symmetric periodic solution trajectories exhibits prevalence among initial values.

The potential of deep learning as a tool for accurately simulating quantum many-body systems through tensor network methods has been explored, and it has been demonstrated that a network can be trained to represent the same ground and excited states as a more time-efficient and computationally efficient qubit model. The training time and errors associated with this learning process were shown to be significantly lower with the qubit model when comparing evolutions of depth 20. However, it was observed that the advantages of the qubit model are lost when the same depth is reached in fermionic evolution models. This indicates that the benefits of the qubit model are closely linked to its ability to avoid the hidden Hamiltonian structure found in fermionic systems. To take advantage of the efficient and accurate nature of the qubit model, a learning network was designed to translate between fermionic and qubit representations of a system. When testing the translation network, it was found to be highly effective, achieving less than 2% error in the representation of a system with 28 qubits following translation from a fermionic representation. Following successful translation, the qubit model was applied to this system, achieving significantly better results than the fermionic model. This includes more precise calculations of the ground and excited state energies as well as more accurate predictions related to the Green's function at a depth of 20. This breakthrough highlights the potential for using deep learning to effectively bridge the gap between fermionic and qubit representations of complex quantum systems.

A key characteristic of deep generative models is the balance between density estimation and representation quality, which affects the balance between maximum likelihood and reconstruction error in the training process. Typically, models like variational autoencoders (VAEs) prioritize flexible representation over high likelihood, while maximum-likelihood optimization is challenging due to the incompatibility of the standard ELBO objective with the exponential family form of a probabilistic decoder. In this context, a new approach called the Deep Generative Decoder (DGD) eliminates the need for a variational approximation, instead offering a fixed, maximum-likelihood optimization framework for a probabilistic decoder with a hidden Markov structure. This leads to the emergence of models with longer memory architectures, enhanced interpretability, and higher performance than VAEs on the same task. The DGD can be combined with a variational encoder to produce the DGD-VAE, which yields better empirical performance than the standard VAE-VAE on several tasks. The DGD is versatile and can be easily adapted to include a variety of supplementary components, such as a discriminative model for rival training or postprocessing noise addition for improved robustness, all while allowing a flexible representation and high likelihood in a variety of tasks.

The discovery of a common-spectrum process in recent NANOGrav findings has led to theories suggesting it could be evidence of a primordial stochastic gravitational-wave background (SGWB) that exceeds expectations based on standard inflation combined with LCDM. If the SGWB exists and is amplified as predicted by the standard inflation + stiff amplification model, which combines the LCDM model with two additional components - a primordial magnetic field and stiff components arising from a phase transition following inflation - this could have significant effects on the expansion history of the universe, potentially alleviating the current Hubble tension. The proposed model reduces the predicted SGWB amplitude by at least an order of magnitude, which aligns with current observations. Meanwhile, estimating the radiation energy density via gravitational-wave spectrum mapping from the SGWB would reduce the LCDM model's tension with CMB radiation energy density constraints by nearly two standard deviations. Additionally, this model offers potential explanations for two observed phenomena - the origin of strong magnetic fields in the universe and the acceleration of the cosmic expansion rate.

Our mission, KOSMA-MKID, in collaboration with the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, successfully detected millimeter-wave emissions originating from a polar comet: C/2015 ER61. By observing the comet on March 2nd and 3rd, 2016, we identified emissions produced by Emission Lines of Glycolysis, Ethanol, Hydrogen Cyanide, and Polycylic organic compounds. Our data not only confirms the presence of previously established molecules like Glycolysis and Ethanol but also reveals the emissions produced by newly discovered substances. Furthermore, we have estimated the mass and flux rates of these molecules. By analyzing the data, we found that the emissions exhibit a linear relationship with the distance from the comet's core and are produced at an average velocity of $\sim$2.6 km/s. Our research is crucial in understanding the emission processes of molecules in comets' atmospheres.

We propose an unsupervised speech synthesis approach that builds on recent research in automatic speech recognition and existing neural-based speech generation methods. Employing only raw, unlabeled audio and text data, as well as a translation dictionary, our technique enables high-quality speech synthesis without requiring a single annotated sample. Human evaluation confirms the synthesized speech produced by the unsupervised system is comparable to that of a traditionally trained model in terms of its naturalness and ease of understanding.

This research employs the Tsallis holographic dark energy model in two scenarios, 
non-interacting and interacting, to calculate essential parameters of the energy 
density equation of state for a flat FLRW universe, including fractional energy 
density and equation of state parameter within the dark energy sector, for both 
 scenarios,  furthermore, power law and quadratic equations of state parameters 
 are specifically calculated,  our results reveal that, for a real universe, the 
 fractional energy density must be confined between zero and one,  furthermore, 
 when the fractional energy density drops below zero it signals a universe in 
 a transition phase,  this research further indicates that,  a universe transition 
 can also be signaled by a negative fractional energy density at a time when 
 the equation of state parameter exceeds one.

Multi-objective mixed-integer non-linear programming problems frequently arise in real-world contexts, notably in mechanical engineering. A novel approach, combining multi-criteria branch-and-bound and non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm 2, is proposed for approximating Pareto fronts for such problems. A computational study, comparing this proposed hybrid method to non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm 2, demonstrates its efficacy with real-world and test cases. A new performance metric, investment ratio, assesses solution quality in relation to computation effort. Results show the proposed hybrid approach outperforms non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm 2 across nearly all performance metrics. Therefore, this proposed hybrid, enhanced with intelligent prey algorithm for guiding evolution, is a suitable solution strategy for mechanical engineering applications.

We refine and reinterpret the core principles of Lie theory, specifically Lie groupoids, through the lens of internal groupoids in synthetic differential geometry. Key concepts are re-expressed, including path sources and integrated $A$-paths. The primary findings demonstrate that a classical Hausdorff Lie groupoid's internal connectivity properties mirror those it satisfies as a classical connected Lie groupoid.

The Dynaswap project is focused on developing a robust, trustworthy architecture for safeguarding holistic workflows in cyberinfrastructures, allowing for deployment on virtual machines via cloud services such as JetStream. This cloud platform facilitates user-friendly access to dynamic computing and data analysis tools on demand. Dynaswap's security architecture incorporates role management, hierarchical relationships, and adaptable access control mechanisms. By integrating cutting-edge frameworks like Authentication-Authorization-Accounting and Blockchain technology, as well as advanced security features, Dynaswap provides a comprehensive protection system. Currently, the Dynaswap architecture is being validated in life-science research and educational settings within the Health Informatics field.

Aspect-based sentiment analysis focuses on determining the sentiment of a particular aspect within product reviews. Approximately one-third of reviews lack explicit opinion words, yet clearly convey human-aware sentiment, classified as implicit sentiment. Unfortunately, neural network-based methods have overlooked implicit sentiment in reviews. To address this, we utilize a supervised pre-training approach on extensive sentiment-annotated datasets drawn from relevant linguistic sources. By aligning implicit sentiment phrases with their matching sentiment labels, this pre-training method significantly improves the capture of both explicit and implicit sentiment orientations in reviews towards a particular aspect. Our technique exhibits superior performance on the SemEval 2014 benchmarks and an in-depth examination demonstrates its effectiveness.

We establish a method to calculate how stratified case-control sampling affects logistic regression parameters related to a secondary outcome of interest. This is particularly significant when conducting mediation analysis with binary outcome and mediator variables in stratified case-control studies. Our results facilitate estimation using M-estimation and Maximum Likelihood methods. A simulation in a real-world scenario shows that the proposed methods maintain decent estimation accuracy. The methods are applied to investigate factors influencing the prevention of mother-to-child transmission of HIV through the use of Antiretroviral Therapy.

This research delves into secure communication systems for multiple users that utilize reconfigurable intelligent surfaces to compensate for hardware limitations.
We simultaneously adjust the base station's beamforming vectors and the phase shifts on the RIS to achieve the highest possible weighted minimum secrecy rate under constraints for the base station's power output as well as RIS element restrictions.
To address this optimization problem, we first split the RIS phase shifts into two parts using an alternating optimization approach.
Next, we transform the original problem into a convex convex convex convex convex convex optimization problem and solve it using the reparameterization technique.
A thorough alternative optimization algorithm is presented to demonstrate the feasibility of this method.
Results showing the impact of varying numbers of RIS elements on the weighted minimum secrecy rate and overall system performance are provided.

We begin by defining a task for few-shot continual learning and propose a theory to explain how executive function works through a self-updating decision-making system that reprocesses perception data through a review of past experiences in order to minimize prediction errors. This idea becomes practical due to the incorporation of a memory mechanism and a pre-trained neural network that is predisposed to follow rules of effective learning and adapts to optimize its chances of long-term success. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our model of executive function can facilitate the development of hypothesis testing as an internal reasoning process and might provide insight into observed abilities of human learning and the organization of the human brain.

We studied the solar wind energy flux near the inner edge of our solar system using data from four different close approaches to the sun by the Parker Solar Probe, where we also recorded contact measurements close to the sun's surface. These approaches took place at an average distance of 28.3 solar radii from the sun and lasted for a combined 29.7 days. During this time, we measured a average energy flux of 5.23 W/m^2, however, our analysis was limited to a specific frequency range of 28-45 solar radii due to changing solar wind patterns outside of this range. To eliminate the influence of core and edge effects, we applied a specific mathematical technique and determined that the solar wind energy flux at 1 solar radius is approximately 19.7 W/m^2, with an associated margin of error. Furthermore, comparing our findings with data from other studies, it appears the solar wind energy flux increases by 1 magnitude as it approaches the sun's inner edge, however, the exact rate and pattern of this increase remains unclear.

In a noncommutative setting, where locally compact Hausdorff groups act on C*-algebras, we introduce the concept of a numerable principal bundle with quantum characteristics. This generalization involves defining a locally trivial G-C*-algebra as a noncommutative analog to the total space of a numerable principal bundle. By building upon the Pedersen ideal's multipliers, we transcend Gelfand-Naimark duality to create this framework. Additionally, when considering compact Hausdorff groups acting on unital C*-algebras, the finiteness of local triviality is equivalent to several conditions, including two covering the definition of a Fock Carlen-Bengtsson C*-algebra. Lastly, when the group action is proper, the spectrum of a proper action C*-algebra coincides with the orbit space of the acting group.

We show that any family of maximal almost-disjoint sets can be destroyed via a specific method of adding new elements that preserves the cardinality of the reals, thereby solving the problem posed by Brendle, an open question in the field.

The introduction of $q$-deformation into optomechanical systems reveals opportunities to amplify non-traditional optical phenomena. This insight drives an investigation of the optical behavior within a linearly coupled $q$-deformed optomechanical system. Composed of two deformed cavities interacting with mechanical mirrors and coupled through a transmission parameter, this study reveals that $q$-deformation enhances the speed and magnitude of phase transitions during optical windows. Furthermore, for a specified range of $q$, these systems exhibit amplification of the optical signal. By manipulating parameters like tunneling strength and optomechanical coupling, one can cause the optical probe to be delayed or advanced by up to milliseconds, with even longer delays achievable through fine-tuning. This work also provides a link between theoretical models of quantum optics based on $q$-deformation and optomechanical experiments, laying the groundwork for $q$-deformation-driven research in optomechanics.

In a previous study, I developed a model where the Two-Rotors Model's negative scissors states, consisting of two-sided classical bodies, exhibited 1 |K| = 1; 0 components and negative space parity. Building on this work, I explored reflections involving rotations of the active rotor. Specifically, I found that if a configuration T satisfies the reflection condition T(2π/a_T) = -T, it can be geodesically rotated to its mirror image, T(-x, -y, z) in the plane containing the rotors' axes. The rotation, which preserves the bodies' shapes, relies on a specific factor, determined by a specific matrix element.

A new method inspired by finite volume schemes leverages a cell-average based neural network to solve partial differential equations. By utilizing the weak formulation of these equations, the method trains a feed-forward network to accurately predict solution evolution between time steps, circumventing traditional numerical limitations. After offline training, the neural network model can be used in conjunction with a finite volume scheme, which requires mesh adaptation. One distinct advantage of this approach is its ability to eliminate CFL restrictions, permitting a wider range of time step sizes. Furthermore, when solving the Heat equation, convergence rates and error magnitudes show dependence on the spatial mesh size while being independent of the time step size. Moreover, the neural network model exhibits exceptional performance in simulating shock waves and rarefaction waves within nonlinear hyperbolic conservation laws with negligible numerical diffusion.

The ALICE Collaboration has finalized the upgrade of its detector, with the current phase involving testing to mark the beginning of data collection for LHC Run 3. In conjunction, studies on the experiment's future are underway, with the primary goal being to enhance ALICE's capabilities to study specific areas, such as the production of heavy flavors and dielectrons with low mass, by doubling the event detection limit. A detailed overview of the experiment's upgraded components, as well as proposed upgrades and plans for future upgrades, will be presented in this report, with a particular focus on the electron identification system utilized in ALICE. In-depth descriptions of key R\&D endeavors for new ALICE components will also be provided. In addition, early results from prototype tests and technical challenges associated with prototype development will be discussed.

The Unruh effect can emerge not only through the entanglement of left and right Rindler regions, but also between forward and backward light cones. Our analysis focuses on the geometric phase arising from this time-related entanglement between the future and past, showing that it can be effectively modelled by a $\Lambda$-system. This provides a new approach to detecting the Unruh effect, offering a different method from traditional Unruh-deWitt detectors. Due to the immense accelerations required by Unruh-deWitt detectors to trigger a response, their experimental verification remains unachieved. Conversely, we showcase that a $\Lambda$-system that is static yet time-dependent can, in principle, detect the timelike Unruh effect using modern technological capabilities.

One of the primary objectives of Information Extraction involves recognizing event descriptions along with their related entities within a given text. This task has received significant attention over the years, yet efforts focused on non-English languages remain largely underrepresented due to a lack of quality datasets required to initiate research. To fill this gap, we have developed a Multilingual Event Extraction dataset containing detailed annotations for over 50,000 event occurrences across 10 languages. This resource not only covers text-based annotations but also incorporates aspect-based sentiment, temporal and qualitative characteristics, making it the largest and most comprehensive dataset in its field to date. Utilizing quality-oriented resources such as Google's Multilingual Semantic Language Model and Wikidata, our dataset strives to strike a balance between density and quality of annotations. Given the substantial scale of our dataset, we are confident that it will play a pivotal role in advancing research in multilingual event extraction. The dataset, along with accompanying codes, will be made available on the MARE project site.

We examine a complex manifold with a Hermitian holomorphic vector bundle and its flag bundles, coupled with their respective universal bundles, now endowed with the induced metrics. A crucial aspect of our research involves establishing the validity, pointwise in Chern forms, of the universal push-forward formula for all universal bundles. A fundamental step toward our proof is explicitly determining, at each point of the flag bundle, the Chern curvature of the universal bundles, as endowed with their induced metrics. This leads to the development of an alternative approach to the Jacobi-Trudi identity using differential forms, as well as confirmation of the positivity of specific Chern forms for Griffiths semipositive vector bundles, thus partially supporting Griffiths' conjecture on characteristic forms of positive characteristic.

Observations from the XMM-Newton telescope revealed how a clumpy stellar wind from a companion star in high mass X-ray binaries impacts the variable absorption and timing properties of the emitted X-rays. We analyzed a 7.22 day dataset for the high mass X-ray binary Steiner 413, which has a donor star with a mass between 6.96 and 9.59 solar masses. We aimed to understand how a stellar wind, known to exist based on UV data analysis, impacts the source's X-ray emissions, particularly its short-term variability, using a comprehensive analysis of the XMM-Newton observations. We identified several transient state episodes in the XMM-Newton observations of Steiner 413, during which the source's variability properties changed significantly. We detected significant absorption variations during these episodes, linked to the wind's edge and the source's local absorption. We compared our findings with a simulation model that mimics a uniform stellar wind. We discovered that the source's fractional variability power at kilohertz frequencies decreases when the wind's speed exceeds 1000 km/s, but this correlation is absent when considering wind speeds below this threshold. Additionally, we found that increased Poincar\'e sigma and autocorrelation function values coincide with the onset of absorption variations at the wind's edge. We observed these timing properties changes prior to notable increases in the absorption. We observed Steiner 413 in a very high state, offering a case study for how clumpy winds impact

The Yang-Mills-aether theory is analyzed to understand the implications of introducing non-abelian aether-like terms that violate Lorentz symmetry, specifically within the framework of perturbative renormalization. Our study focuses on the gauge theory's stability and its self-interactions under Lorentz-covariant renormalization, along with other physical parameters. Our key findings reveal that non-abelian terms do not add new ultraviolet divergences compared to their abelian counterparts, but they do result in interaction terms linking the aether field to gauge bosons, differing from the standard Maxwell-Chern-Simons terms. These results indicate that, to comply with observational evidence demanding galactic scale invariant curvature bounds on aether, extremely tight constraints must be imposed on the dimensionless coupling constants of the Yang-Mills-aether theory, specifically on the ratio of the aether coupling constant to the Yang-Mills coupling constant.

Researchers have long sought to bridge the gap between syntax and semantics parsing but so far have had to make a choice between excelling in one area at the cost of the other, contradicting research highlighting the complex interactions between the two. To address this issue, we examine multiple model designs capable of tapping into rich data in the Universal Decompositional Semantics (UDS) dataset to aid unified parsing, comparing their effectiveness with that of cutting-edge parsing models trained solely on corresponding raw semantic data. Our findings reveal that integrating syntax and semantics or modeling them concurrently yields superior results than parsing them separately. Moreover, we discover that leveraging semantics derived from semantic graphs, as opposed to raw data, leads to substantial improvements. These insights suggest the beneficial use of semantics from ground truth semantic graphs to enhance parsing performance.

The formation of magnetically-driven jets from a spinning black hole following a compact binary merger is a potentially significant event, capable of launching outflows that explain the phenomenon of kilonovae radiation and graviational wave disc fragmentation. We have observed this process in detail using simulations of the initial 10 milliseconds after merger. Our simulations, which employed a 2D axisymmetric simulation code, assumed a dipole magnetic field initial condition and consistent hydrodynamics. We discovered that the mass ejected from the black hole equator shows a linear relationship with the black hole's spin rate. Furthermore, the mass ejected from the black hole equator shows a linear relationship with the black hole's mass ejected across all scenarios. Our simulations reveal that magnetically-driven jets can transport at least one mass equivalent of $10^{-5}$ times the merged cloud's solar mass away from the black hole's equator as an accretion disc around the newly formed black hole.

We undertook a statistical investigation into tidal features surrounding early-type galaxies of massive proportions, utilizing data from the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program. Our analysis revealed that roughly 28 percent of 2649 galaxies, selected due to their mass greater than $10^{11}M_{\odot}$ and within a redshift range of 0.05-0.15, exhibited distinct tidal features exceeding one percent flux fraction. Observations indicated an exponential decline in the number of galaxies as tidal features became more pronounced. Additionally, within our defined stellar mass scope, we observed tidal features increase in frequency by two-fold when shifting from $10^{11}M_{\odot}$ to $10^{12}M_{\odot}$. A thorough analysis including pair-counts to estimate the merging rate of massive early-type galaxies revealed that tidal features persist for a duration of approximately 3 billion years. This outcome was found to align with findings from prior studies.

This paper is a component of a research series focusing on the Azimuthally Symmetric Theory of Gravitation (ASTG), a theoretical framework derived from the established equation by Laplace and Poisson. Our findings indicate that, under specific conditions dependent on the object's spin, the ASTG can generate repulsive gravitational fields in the polar regions of massive objects, thereby shedding new light on the phenomenon of outflows as a manifestation of repulsive gravity. This process is an integral component of star formation and has been the subject of extensive debate regarding its origins. This paper diverges from the conventional understanding of gravitation, presenting it as a force that, in certain contexts, drives material apart rather than pulling it together towards a central point. Furthermore, we present empirical evidence that suggests the Azimuthally Symmetric Gravitational Field derived from the ASTG can effectively explain recently discovered phenomena including the gravitational repulsion observed in Sgr A* and the spiral, arched, and circular shapes of CO emission in the vicinity of the Sgr A* supermassive black hole as well as features like the radial motion of molecular clouds in the center of NGC 1068.

We have gathered a vast data set of 81 fast radio burst observations from the literature. Our analysis is the most extensive compilation of optical data from both published and unpublished sources. Our research establishes a threshold for optical flare radiation at 42,000 solar levels. Specifically, we measured the optical flux of the repeating FRB 20201124 using the optical spectrograph OSIRIS and the photometer Taos, resulting in observed values of 2.0 x 10^-12 erg/cm^2/s at 4500 Angstroms and 1.2 x 10^-12 erg/cm^2/s at 6500 Angstroms, respectively. Our observations also provide new insights into the optical emission patterns of FRBs, suggesting a connection between sudden optical flares and radio bursts. Furthermore, the optical data impose strict limits on the radiation energy released in the radio bursts, favoring non-thermal models. Our results also indicate that a significant amount of ionized gas, possibly associated with the local galactic environment, is required to explain the optical observations of FRB 20201124.

The combination of chirped pulse amplification and nonlinear optical systems has been the foundation for significant progress in numerous sectors, including semiconductors, communications, biology, defense, and national security. However, accurately modeling these laser systems using CPA and NLO is a complex task due to their interconnected linear and nonlinear processes, and the high variability in available modeling frameworks. The absence of a unified software platform for CPA-NLO modeling restricts further development and potential implementation of these systems in data-driven approaches such as inverse design. We introduce a modular software model that encompasses various amplifier configurations and nonlinear techniques to provide time and frequency-resolved electromagnetic field data and essential physical properties, enabling characteristics of the radiation produced by these laser systems to be simulated. The new software offers a unified platform for capturing the complex interactions within CPA-NLO systems and generating high-resolution field data. Additionally, we showcase the potential of our software by applying it to the design of a laser source optimized for free-electron laser (FEL) seeding, where a comprehensive comparison with third-party code validates the developed model.

Multimodal language generation capabilities of models like GPT-2 and GPT-3 can be leveraged for producing high-quality text, but it is still uncertain how they can be directed by non-text modalities like images. We introduce a new framework called MAGIC that allows these models to perform tasks such as image captioning in the absence of explicit training data. By combining an existing language model like GPT-2 with an image-text matching model like CLIP, MAGIC provides a plug-and-play solution that guides the model's output during generation. MAGIC's unique approach introduces a regularization factor, known as the "magic score", that gauges how well the generated text describes an image without seeing the image itself during the process. We evaluated MAGIC on various versions of XQuadruplet, image captioning, and visual question answering and discovered that it successfully yields state-of-the-art or near state-of-the-art outcomes on the XQuadruplet and image captioning benchmarks while performing more efficiently than the direct application of GPT-2, also surpassing the current leading solutions on visual question answering.

We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports stealth addresses in conjunction with Delegated Proof of Stake, resulting in Delegated RingCT.
The Delegated RingCT scheme is comprised of an integrated signature and encryption framework, combining a public key encryption protocol and two types of signatures along with linkable ring signatures, alongside non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs.
A comprehensive description of Delegated RingCT, along with security evidence and an implemented prototype, are presented, which we subsequently test through benchmarking analysis.
While Delegated RingCT may not possess the same level of anonymity compared to other RingCT implementations, we propose that its ability to be compatible with DPoS constitutes a significant advancement in the realm of decentralized cryptocurrencies, offering a considerable reduction in latency and increased consensus speeds, ultimately enabling scalable anonymity in distributed systems.

In 2015, CERN introduced "Emittance Scans," a new fast luminosity separation scanning method at the Large Hadron Collider. These scans were consistently carried out during physics production runs, utilizing full-intensity beams at the CMS experiment's interaction point. The emittance scans allowed for rapid, in-situ beam measurement and performance diagnosis, incorporating auto-focused beam patterns and quantitative beam measurements. Additionally, these scans facilitated improvements at the CMS experiment through a joint effort in joint beam studies, demonstrating the effectiveness of this approach in enhancing LHC performance and the CMS experiment through joint beam studies.

Recent breakthroughs in artificial neural networks have accelerated the growth of data-driven modeling in mechanics, making cooperative modeling more feasible. As research advances, diverse teams can create new models and data while preserving their independence, collaboration, and innovation. Nevertheless, continual learning techniques are restricted due to the phenomenon of catastrophic forgetting, which remains a critical challenge for cooperative modeling. We explore the potential of advanced machine learning methods, specifically the ensemble averaging technique, to combat catastrophic forgetting. By testing the approach with simulations and real-world experiments, we evaluate its efficacy and efficiency in the context of cooperative modeling. Our results indicate that the ensemble averaging technique could facilitate cooperative modeling by reducing or eliminating catastrophic forgetting, although it may come with limitations in terms of computational resource usage. Ultimately, further research is needed to refine this strategy and develop more efficient distributed techniques for cooperative modeling.

This research examines the decay of the $\Upsilon(10753)$ into a $\Upsilon(nS)$
state accompanied by $\pi^+\pi^-$ particles, where $n=1,2,3$. It's assumed
$\Upsilon(10753)$ belongs to a typical bottomonium under the $4S$-$3D$ mixing
scenario. We find that these specific decay processes have relatively large
branching ratios of $10^{-4}$ to $10^{-3}$ and, notably, align with Belle's
experimental findings, validating our previous assignment of the $\Upsilon(10753)$
bottomonium to the $4S$-$3D$ mixing scheme. Further validation of this work
could be achieved through testing with Belle II experiment data.

This paper presents a novel optimization technique called AskewSGD to efficiently train deep neural networks with quantized weights. Initially, neural network parameters are randomly initialized in the standard manner, then continuously updated and optimized using AskewSGD, where the quantization operation occurs between each iteration. The theoretical foundation of AskewSGD is built upon a conventional gradient descent method, which is reformulated to be applicable with quantized parameters. The resulting algorithm allows the use of established training methods, originally devised for floating-point parameters, on neural networks with quantized weights. AskewSGD's effectiveness has been demonstrated through comprehensive testing on the ImageNet dataset for various neural network architectures and quantization schemes, showing remarkable compatibility and performance competitiveness with respect to other optimization methods.

The Continuum Soft Robot project utilizes fully flexible mechanical systems to achieve robots that more closely resemble the anatomy of invertebrate creatures and flexible body parts of vertebrates. To introduce the concepts and challenges of this innovative area in robotics, we will be adopting a control theorist's approach, simplifying the entry into this field by systematically presenting current research and future obstacles through a uniform language and organized structure. The primary hurdles to participating in this area are the vast differences in terminology and the disjointed nature of the research, leading to an overview of key technological hurdles in continuum robotics, categorized as intrinsic and data-related challenges, and a survey of the current state of the art in modeling and experimentation. The paper will provide an intrinsic analysis of these issues, focusing on experimental control methods for continuum robotics and highlighting key aspects for robot design, control approaches, and observation problems. The research aims to create a comprehensive understanding of the complexities involved in controlling these innovative robots, enabling a standardized standard to be established and simplifying the analysis of this area for the community.

The Jacobi group $G^J_1(\mathbb{R})$ - specifically its semi-direct product of ${\rm SL}(2,\mathbb{R})$ with $H^1$ - can be embedded into a realisation of ${\rm Sp}(2,\mathbb{R})$ via a 4-dimensional representation, which preserves the Kleinian recursion and the Hilbert-Poincaré metric. Consequently, this embedding propagates the action of $G^J_1(\mathbb{R})$ on the Schottky Green's function and the Schottky coordinates, ultimately revealing an invariant metric on the Schottky space. Notably, this metric exhibits a infinite curvature at every point as a result of its Kobayashi-Hitchin norm being identically zero. Similar phenomena can be observed with Poincaré metric on hyperbolic upper half-plane and extremal Kobayashi-Hitchin norms on ${\rm SL}(2,\mathbb{R})$'s left-invariant complex structures.

Verifying facts using structured data can be complicated by intricate relationships between them, as conventional approaches often employ simple, multi-partner affiliations. To tackle this, we've developed a novel framework incorporating relationship-specific temporal constraints, by making the verification process ask if the relationships between the facts happened one after the other. This method utilizes both spatial and temporal cues from knowledge graphs to determine the feasibility of the verified claims. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, we've designed a suitable dataset representing claims and annotated it with precise temporal references. Our technique outperforms established methods on all fronts and contributes significantly to understanding the verification of multi-dimensional factual information. Code and the newly created dataset are publicly available for further research.

The state of the art in learned synthetic image generation involves generative adversarial networks. Initial breakthroughs relied solely on unlabelled data, but subsequent advances incorporated large quantities of ground truth depth maps and scene flow. Although programmes like LINDENCI and PUG-Net utilise detailed datasets and specialised hardware, a novel approach in our research utilises a simplified programme to create diverse scenes and trains a neural network to generate coloured images using only three rendered depth maps, all without requiring any additional labels or specialised equipment. Notably, our results surpass the state of the art in several metrics, particularly in the challenging driving scenario dataset.

To perform Bayesian inference using nested sampling, a specific prior sampling approach must be used, which involves selecting prior samples that meet a minimum likelihood requirement. Researchers have developed methods like Markov Chain Monte Carlo derivatives for complex, high-dimensional problems. A study examined ten different algorithms, incorporating techniques from slice sampling, hit-and-run, and differential evolution, to determine their efficiency in various dimensions and at different likelihood levels. Contrary to initial expectations, simple methods often performed better than more complex variations. Additionally, incorporating MCMC moves resulted in consistent scalability, regardless of the algorithm used, but led to reduced efficiency compared to static sampling methods. A set of C++-based sampling algorithms is now available online as an open-source package.

In fault-tolerant distance labelling, we're tasked with assigning brief descriptions to the points in a network so that knowing any three points allows us to deduce the distance between any two of them, excluding the third. Our work proves that any weighted network with a specific layout (or in fact any network with limited separating elements) allows for labelling that uses a logarithmic amount of information, with an added ability to disregard up to one incorrect input in calculating distances. This solves a key problem in data science and yields novel results for the underlying topics of fault-tolerant distance labelling and network topology discovery.

The underlying dynamics of two-particle correlations is crucial for understanding the behavior of these correlations as they evolve over time. By focusing on specific impurity levels in the one-dimensional Hubbard model, researchers study the oscillations within the two-particle correlation function within the adiabatic regime. Within this regime, a particular computational approach reveals the details of prethermalized states that consist of multiple separated bands. By analyzing how these bands behave, the researchers are able to determine the general pattern of oscillations based on the imaginary part of a complex matrix, known as the Liouvillian gap. This pattern holds significant importance as it can be used to determine the rate at which heat is transferred within the system, making it a valuable area of study. By applying additional mathematical analyses, the full set of equations governing the impurity levels is established, providing a solid understanding of how these levels behave over time, thereby solidifying the established pattern of oscillations. This research not only provides a solid understanding of the existing model but also serves as a starting point for exploring similar behaviors within more complex models, such as models that incorporate two extra dimensions, with interesting applications in systems of interacting fermions, such as superconductors and cold atoms, as well as photo-assisted systems.

For a given second-order linear elliptic equation with coefficients $A$, $\mathbf{b}$ and a parameter $\lambda$, defined within a bounded $\mathbb{R}^2$ domain $\Omega$ and satisfying specific regularity and conditionality requirements, we establish existence and uniqueness of the weak solution in $W^{1,p}(\Omega)$ for the parameterized problem $-\text{div}(A(x,\lambda)\nabla u)+\lambda\phi=\mu$ along with the boundary condition $u=\0$ on $\partial\Omega$.

To ensure that medical imaging models produce accurate predictions, it is crucial to implement out-of-distribution detection capabilities. This particular model investigates out-of-distribution detection in brain tumor segmentation tasks, identifying the patient's age and tumor location as relevant input factors. By utilizing a pre-trained classification network, they developed an unsupervised out-of-distribution detection system that identifies anomalous age ranges and tumor locations. The proposed approach, detailed in a paper titled "Identifying Unusual Brain Tumors using Unusual Patient Characteristics," showcases the effectiveness of this method in detecting outliers in age and spatial clusters of brain tumors.

Quantum systems driven periodically experience heat build-up due to resonant excitations, typically leading to a random thermal state. In contrast, a system that is both driven and in contact with a heat bath will instead converge towards a distinct, out-of-balance stable condition. Our study shows that an interplay between periodic stimulation and interaction with a heat bath gives rise to a phenomenon we've called out-of-balance thermalization. By using an optical cavity as a test area, where the stimulation causes a resonant modulation in the cavity-resonator system coupled to a bath of optical modes, we've observed this phenomenon and studied its characteristics in detail, rather than the system as a whole. Instead, a controlled approach is taken, focusing on a single, continuously evolving component of the stimulated system and revealing a distinct transition from random thermal behavior to out-of-balance thermal behavior under stimulation, as observed in the continuously evolving component of the stimulated system.

The article explores the convex solution $u$ of the Helfrich equation $$-\nabla\cdot\frac{\nabla u}{\cosh^2(\sqrt{\alpha})u}=\alpha$$ with nonpositive boundary data in a half-space $\alpha\in (0,1)$ by proving two main points. Firstly, we establish that $u$ satisfies an Alexandrov maximum principle and is Holder continuous for a specific range of values. Secondly, we decompose the convex solution $u$ into two convex solutions $u_1$ and $u_2$ of the minimal surface equation, with minimal and maximal values defined as $u(0)=0$ and $u(x,0)=0$ respectively. This allows us to derive an minimal surface equation for the minimal graph $u_1(x,y)$ and a quadratic equation for the maximal graph $u_2(x,y)$ with maxima at $(0,0)$ for $u_1$ and $(x,0)$ for $u_2$.

Counting the recurrence of periodic events allows us to measure time. Historically, developing stable and accurate timekeeping devices was a significant undertaking. We will instead examine a different class of timekeeping devices, based on random clicking mechanisms. A comprehensive statistical analysis framework is developed to evaluate the effectiveness of these devices, with specific examples being ensembles of clicker, diffusive, and flow-controlled systems. A key benefit of these random timekeepers is their resistance to degradation due to interference, alongside their substantial time-keeping accuracies. We further introduce a concept for constructing logical operations using these random timekeepers, where deterministic logic circuits can be generated from probabilistic ones by enhancing their resolution. The probability of correctly obtained outputs is evaluated, specifically for AND, OR, and NOT gates, with relevant applications in neural interfaces, sensor technology, and time measurement.

This research centers on Software Defined Networks (SDN) to address the challenges of traffic engineering, fault prevention, and service delivery within reliability and energy constraints. Utilizing Fog computing, we focus on optimizing distributed traffic flows in multi-domain networks based on fault-tolerant criteria, coupled with constrained resource management at the fog level. Our proposed architecture, Fog-SDN-OC, incorporates an overlay architecture at the fog level to harmonize control and data planes, thereby facilitating fault-tolerant network design. The network design problem is formulated as a mixed-integer linear programming problem, which is solved through cooperative game theory and the Proximal Decomposition algorithm. The effectiveness of our approach was demonstrated using the Grid5000 testbed and the INES-FGI dataset. The network design provided by Fog-SDN-OC outperformed other strategies in terms of network durability, energy efficiency, and overall network performance. Additionally, we evaluated the coefficients of variation for flow redistribution and network congestion during node failures, thereby validating their potential through empirical calculations.

Metric learning's pair-wise loss technique is centered around optimizing an embedding that maximizes similarity between images within the same class, minimizing distance between images in distinct classes. Various forms of pair-wise loss strategies have been proposed. To consolidate this diverse set of loss functions, we've isolated specific aspects that dictate how these functions manipulate the positioning of feature pairs. Breaking down pair-wise gradient updates this way enables a deeper understanding of the dominant effects and allows for the development of a streamlined algorithm, ultimately leading to better image retrieval performance across datasets like CAR, CUB, and the Stanford Online Marketplace.

In this research, we explore certain classes of holographic tensor networks, which can efficiently simulate various systems using the principle of minimization, serve as quantum codes against noise, and accurately depict dynamics resulting from non-trivial interactions. The work demonstrates that these networks, comprising generalized hydrodynamic tensors, can be effectively modeled using a finite set of basic tensors through an entanglement-squeezing procedure. Furthermore, it is found that networks composed of 4-valent CA toxins, implementing quantum codes against correlated noise, can be directly equivalent to networks composed of 4-valent hydrodynamic causal states. A comprehensive overview of the underlying principles and mechanics is provided, and a few examples and potential applications of these networks are examined.

Our research centred on magnetized radio filaments in the Galactic centre, specifically those observed by FERMI CRAFT and also examined in 4.5 GHz studies by Tisjar et al. These filament groups, often featuring looped or hairpin-shaped magnetic fields, are divided into two categories based on their relative angles to the galactic plane. Both categories display similar properties and shapes, yet the filament groups differ in their orientation to the galactic plane. We identified 15 grouped filament formations through FERMI CRAFT data and categorized them based on their angle to the galactic plane: 11 objects with a 28 degree margin and 4 objects with an 8 degree margin. We calculated the distances between the grouped filaments and their proximity to 30 day-care sources, as well as their angular separation from the supermassive black hole at the galactic centre. We observed a pattern suggesting the grouped filaments tend to be closer to Sgr A* at the galactic centre when they are oriented towards the galactic plane. We further discovered a correlation between the distance to Sgr A* and the distance between the grouped filaments, specifically those in the 28 degree category. We discuss the potential role of the supermassive black hole in the galactic centre as a driver of the structural arrangement of these grouped magnetized radio filaments.

A proposed paper suggests a new method of distributed leader-follower control for achieving conservation voltage reduction in unbalanced three-phase distribution systems by optimizing DERs through the scheduling of smart inverters. The method considers primary-secondary networks and loads influenced by voltage. The system is modeled using the Peruvian distribution system, and results compared to existing approaches demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in maintaining system stability and achieving optimal conservation voltage reduction.

We investigate non-stochastic bandits and experts in a delayed context, where delays are contingent upon both the time and arm choice. While delayed settings with time-dependent delays have been thoroughly studied, considering arm-dependent delays is more reflective of real-world applications, but raises additional technical obstacles.
