Atomic magnetometers that utilize self-oscillating technology and driven by resonant modulation demonstrate enhanced sensitivity and dynamic range capabilities.
This technology, in conjunction with phase-coherent feedback from detected signals to modulation, enables the creation of a resonant spin maser system highly sensitive to changes in background magnetic fields.
Our system incorporates digital signal processing integrated into the maser feedback loop, thereby meeting the necessary phase condition for resonant precession.
Using a compact laser and mass-produced caesium vapour cell, it functions effectively in a 50 microtesla field and has the potential to be applied in portable geophysical magnetic field measurements.
Our results show a Cramer-Rao limited resolution of 50 fT at 1 second sampling rate and a 10 kHz bandwidth, indicating a suitable resolution for precise measurements.
This technology represents an innovative type of atomic system, capable of competing with conventional magnetometers used for geophysical magnetic field measurements, as well as offering promising possibilities for phase-stable atomic clock systems.

For K3 surfaces with an automorphism having a Siegel disk, the identity component of its group of automorphisms is topologically rational. It is proven that the number of generators of its Picard group cannot exceed three, unless the surface is already defined over the rational numbers, in which case the upper limit can be disregarded. This conclusion stems from the understanding that K3 surfaces with an automorphism in the identity component never become rational when the field of definition is modified, whereas K3 surfaces carrying only the identity automorphism never contain any Siegel disks. Furthermore, as previously established, K3 surface Picard groups cannot be generated by just one element. An additional finding is that K3 surfaces carrying Siegel disks and defined over the rational numbers are uniquely defined by their Picard number, which, interestingly, coincides with the number of generators of their Picard group in this specific context.

A supergravity unified framework neutralino is proposed as a plausible candidate for dark matter, where a long-lived neutralino decays into the hidden sector's lightest supersymmetric particle, exceeding the age of the universe. We introduce an extension to the MSSM/SUGRA model with a $U(1)_{X_1} \times U(1)_{X_2}$ hidden sector gauge sector, where the hidden sector neutralino is lighter than its visible counterpart, leading to a loop-suppressed radiative decay process. The computation reveals that the visible sector neutralino can decay with a lifetime greater than the age of the universe. The detectability of this scenario lies in the second generation's visible sector neutralino's decay into the hidden sector neutralino, resulting in a characteristic sub-GeV monochromatic neutrino spectrum. The model further includes a hidden sector higgsino that acquires a vev, contributing to the hidden sector neutralino's mass, influencing the dark matter density through the visible sector neutralino's annihilation into the hidden sector neutralino, demonstrating the model's sensitivity to the hidden sector's mass parameter, thereby avoiding cosmological constraints. The second generation's visible sector neutralino's relevance to the dark matter density is reduced as the hidden sector neutralino's mass increases.

The main contributions of this study include developing an Efficient Polynomial-Time Approximation Scheme for finding the minimum surface packing number of a given surface-embedded graph, and proving the hardness of finding an exact surface packing number for such graphs, both in terms of theoretical complexity and practical time requirements.

A stochastic Newton algorithm for distributed convex optimization tasks is proposed, which utilizes individual machine capabilities to calculate gradient and Hessian-vector products of cost functions, while the master node orchestrates the sampling process and designates communication tasks. Convergence analysis is performed within a variational condition that encompasses stochastic Newton errors, communication delays, and individual data sets, ultimately showing super-Nester methods can lead to improved performance. Additionally, experimental results validate the algorithm's efficacy in comparison to existing methods, such as AIDE, PROST, and SDG, on a range of tasks including logistic regression and quadratic learning.

Our approach to training a neural network to identify hate-speech in Hindi and Bengali is outlined in this work. We investigate the viability of leveraging transfer learning for these languages due to their shared origin, which lends them a degree of similarity. Our experiment's implementation on low-powered hardware yields results that hold up against those of more costly models, a noteworthy finding. Additionally, given the limited training data and our unfamiliarity with these languages, our study represents an attempt to decipher languages often shrouded in mystery.

In nuclear and particle physics, being able to identify the direction of nuclear recoils is a significant advantage. This capability, achievable at low energies, could help verify that a dark matter signal originates from space, surpass the neutrino floor, or distinguish between various neutrino sources. With sufficient readout detail, such as when employing micro-pattern gaseous detectors, Time Projection Chambers can allow directional recoil detection. The main issue with these detectors is identifying and eliminating background electron recoils triggered by gamma rays from radioactive substances within the detector and surroundings. We created new indicators that can tell electron and nuclear recoils apart at keV-level energies by using simulated ionization topologies. Our simulation shows that these indicators perform significantly better than the traditionally used dE/dx discriminant, offering up to three times greater differentiation. Additionally, these new indicators remain effective at lower ionization levels below 10 keV and remain resilient when the detector's direction-finding ability fails.

A comprehensive analysis of commercial driving behavior requires considering various personal characteristics and environmental influences like weather and road conditions. Current driver-assessment systems, relying solely on behavior data, may yield unfair and inaccurate results by neglecting contextual factors. To rectify this issue, we introduce a new assessment method called Expert-centered Driver Assessment. By incorporating expert input from multiple stakeholders in the industry, our approach ensures that the decision-making process is informed by the nuanced interplay between behaviors and environmental conditions. Based on a literature review and expert consultation, we identified crucial factors impacting driving behavior and designed an uncertainty-reflective questionnaire format to capture experts' diverse views. Fuzzy set modeling enabled us to incorporate these uncertainties into our analysis. The proposed method allowed us to identify key contextual factors and effectively integrate experts' opinions into our driver-assessment model, as exemplified by our case study using feedback from Heavy Goods Vehicles professionals.

This paper reports on the findings from the 2022 Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) challenge.
The competition highlighted an underinvestigated area in Optical Character Recognition (OCR) technology: accurately reading previously unseen text in real-world images during model training.
The dataset compiled for the competition comprises a diverse collection of 326,385 images, encompassing 4,864,405 text instances.
To address the challenge, a distinct validation and test set was created, comprising scene text that was not present in the training data.
The competition featured two recognition tasks: a holistic approach to reading full text and a focused task involving cropped text segments.
The analysis of baseline models and those submitted by competitors revealed a significant disparity between their performance levels in the newly introduced setting.
The proposed dataset and framework are now offered as a resource to the community for further research into this critical yet understudied topic.
Ultimately, successful development of Generalized OCR models capable of reading novel, unseen text during the training and deployment phase holds the potential to significantly elevate the versatility and practicality of text detection and recognition technology.

Random fields in mathematical models depict how interconnected random variables behave over time, influencing a variety of disciplines from statistical physics to system biology. Since their introduction in the 19th century, little has been known about the link between their dynamic behaviors and geometric properties of the underlying spaces they're defined within. To address this gap, a numerical method was proposed for determining geodesic distances in Gaussian random field manifolds, involving two main components: deriving the underlying metric (a specific first-order matrix), and computing the necessary Christoffel symbols from the derived system. These calculations are used to solve the resulting system of differential equations through iterative approaches, such as Runge-Kutta. The method was further validated by comparing geodesic distance estimates with numerical simulations and actual data from Michael's experiment, demonstrating strong correspondence between the predicted outcomes and actual results.
In our research, we conduct experiments on Rayleigh-Taylor Instability by introducing a controlled disturbance through magnetic levitation technology.

For a cuspidal Hecke-Maass oldform L-function, we establish the boundedness of the algebraic component at critical points. This achievement is achieved utilizing the contrast between the rank of cuspform sequences, derived from the unique cuspform or its dual, and the depth of cuspform sequences, gained through the application of the Coleff-Huet-Witt residue operator in combination with the power series expansion of the L-function. Building upon this work, we establish the L^p integrality of the Euler product representation of the L-function over a compact interval of p-adic integers less than p, specifically within the range [1/2p, 1/(2p^2)).

In a tight binding model using the non-equilibrium Green's functions formalism, researchers explored how spin-dependent transport behaves in armchair graphene nanoribbons with ferromagnetic gate control, and how it's influenced by device geometry and contact position. Various combinations of device parameters were simulated to investigate spin injection and Hall effects. The findings showed that nanoribbons with wide band gaps exhibit noticeable spin polarization, which can be adjusted by adjusting the gate voltage to obtain high, reversible spin injection and accurate measurement of the spin Hall conductivity in these ribbons.

This paper presents proofs of Korovkin theorem analogues in the realm of weakly nonlinear, monotone operators applied to multi-variable Banach lattices of functions. Our study encompasses the almost everywhere convergence, convergence in measure, and $L^{p}$-norm convergence. The discussion is supplemented by several examples that demonstrate the theoretical findings.

A graph on n vertices is called pancyclic if it contains a cycle of every possible length from 3 to n. Research by Chao and Liu revealed that a graph T on n vertices being pancyclic depends on certain criteria involving the p-degree of T, which is the sum of the p-element subgraph sizes in T. Building upon the work of Chao and Liu, further research by Liu considered similar dependencies for a graph being cyclic of a specific order. This paper aims to extend and strengthen these previous results, focusing on the concept of p-splitting number ps, which represents the minimum number of p-element subgraphs required for a graph G to have a p-element cycle. The study then establishes a lower bound for ps in terms of the p-degree d of graph G and demonstrates its applicability to a previously existing conjecture concerning pancyclic graphs.

The trajectory of light particles created in gold-gold, ruthenium-ruthenium, and zirconium-zirconium collisions at a specific energy level of 200 GeV has been studied in this research. This study utilized the CLVisc model to examine the development of uneven energy distribution in the system and its influence on the direction of light particles emitted. By analyzing these findings along with previous data on heavier ions, researchers were able to explore the relationship between the degree of uneven energy distribution and the number of participants in the collision. Ultimately, the study's outcomes revealed that the uneven energy distribution plays a significant role in the direction of light particles moved.

The adaptive spectral Koopman method was designed to solve complex autonomous dynamical systems that serve as the groundwork for numerous applications across various scientific and engineering fields. Despite its high performance in solving systems of any dimension via time-invariant equations, ASK faces challenges when dealing with systems that require time-varying solutions. To overcome this limitation, a new technique was developed to apply the Koopman operator differently at various time intervals, resulting in the proposed sparse-grid-based ASK method. By using a combination of ASK and sparse grid techniques, this approach significantly reduces the computational complexity of solving time-varying systems, thus enabling faster computation on higher-dimensional systems in particular. To evaluate its performance, simulations of different systems at various dimensions were performed and the results compared with time-invariant methods, showing the proposed method's high accuracy and significant computational speed improvements.

This paper builds upon previous research by S. M. Saez and J. R. Hibbert, which appeared in Proc. R. Soc. A, 477:2019. Their initial findings identified resonance parameters in one-dimensional quantum mechanics and proposed a new approach for determining them in any dimension. Our present work focuses on validating the method using different potential functions in one and two dimensions.

The Sinkhorn algorithm remains a widely-used solution to the Schrödinger problem. While it's well-documented that this algorithm converges when a solution exists, a linear convergence rate is achieved only if both the solution and the reference coupling have the same support. Considering that structured stochastic processes may result in degenerate scenarios where the solution does not exist, research demonstrates that even in such situations, the Sinkhorn algorithm leads to two specific points of convergence. Crucially, these limit points enable the calculation of a solution to a more relaxed version of the original problem. The relaxed version can be thought of as the result of replacing the original problem's marginal constraints with marginal penalizations in a related problem. As a result of these findings, a new theoretical framework has been established that allows for the determination of the solution support in both the original and the relaxed problem for any reference coupling and marginal constraints. We demonstrate the potential effectiveness of this theoretical framework through a promising application in a cell biology model.

The ATLAS experiment at the LHC recorded data of 257 pb-1 in proton-proton collisions at a 5.02 TeV centre-of-mass energy in 2017, which is utilized to determine the t¯t cross-section. The measurement involves both t¯t leptonics and non-jectiles modes, amounting to a total σ(t¯t) = 43.6 pb (statistical error: 7.3 pb, systematic error: 3.8 pb, overall error: 10.6 pb). This result is consistent with theoretical predictions from fifth-order QCD, namely ATLAS note TN-03-001 σ(t¯t) pred = 43.5 pb.

It's logical to assume that the characteristics of a surrounding system or environment would influence the behavior of its core element. Researchers have recently investigated the impact of this phenomenon in many-body localized systems, which maintain individualized behavior despite being coupled to a central degree of freedom. In a related area of study, the central degree of freedom was itself composed of multiple parts. Researchers have now used both theoretical and numerical methods to examine what occurs when a central degree of frequency $\omega_0$ is coupled to a one-dimensional system that is disordered and interacting with multiple sites. They found that the central degree of freedom exhibited distinct patterns in its dynamics and spectral behavior. Furthermore, the dynamics of the central degree of frequency $\omega_0$ displayed non-exponential behavior and its spectral behavior displayed the emergence of a resonance peak. Additionally, the data showed that energy transmission between the central degree of frequency $\omega_0$ and the surrounding system was not restricted by spatial or time-based constraints. Their work also revealed that the central degree of frequency $\omega_0$ could be used as a means of controlling and influencing the dynamics of the surrounding system. Ultimately, the data presented a comprehensive view of the relationship between the central degree of frequency $\omega_0$ and the surrounding system.

The conditions on $A$, $B$, $p$, $b$, and $c$ are specified that guarantee 
${u}_{p,b,c}(z)$ meets the requirement ${u}_{p,b,c}(z) \prec (1+Az)/(1+Bz)$. This yields conditions 
for $(-4\kappa/c)({u}_{p,b,c}(z)-1)$, $c \neq 0$, to be close-to-closed related to $(1+Bz)/A$, 
and for ${u}_{p,b,c}(z)$ to be close-to-closed related to $(1+Bz)/A$, given $A$, $B$, and $c$ are positive real numbers. Several examples are provided.

Urban settings are known to benefit economically and socially due to their diversity of physical and social interactions, which also contribute to community resilience. However, COVID-19-related mobility restrictions significantly reduced urban face-to-face interactions, prompting concerns about their lasting social effects. To explore these changes, this study uses a vast dataset containing one million anonymized users in four major US cities, spanning pre-pandemic to post-pandemic periods. It reveals a significant drop (by 15% to 30%) in urban diversity during the pandemic and into late 2021, despite overall mobility rates recovering to pre-pandemic levels. Furthermore, counterfactual analysis shows that the primary factors contributing to decreased diversity included increased home isolation and lower willingness to explore new places, with altered visitation preferences exacerbating the decline over time. Consequently, it is observed that the reduced diversity diversity is linked to decreased emotional states in urban settings. It is hypothesized that long-term social effects will manifest as decreased innovation in urban settings, a relationship that this study preliminary confirms. Future research will seek to elicit further details, including potential gender-based disparities in urban diversity and its impact on innovation rates.

This research project focuses on the advancement of a nonlinear field-split
preconditioner comprising two stages to expedite convergence of complex two-phase
fluid dynamics and transport within diverse porous media. A proposed algorithm,
Field Split NPSI, separates the nonlinear two-phase flow and transport equations into
two individual, loosely coupled systems that can be easily solved at reduced cost.
First, the system of pressure solves interacts with the boundary conditions to
match pressure across cell boundaries, effectively isolating and solving transport
equations efficiently using a Dirac delta function as a source term. Subsequently,
the system of heads is then used to determine superimposed pressure profiles for the
subsequent iteration. A numerical experiment comparing Field Split NPSI with
standard Newton's method showed substantial improvement in computational efficiency
for Field Split NPSI. Given its success in loosely coupling two-phase flow and
transport equations efficiently, Field Split NPSI provides an ideal approach for the
simulation of diverse porous media models. Due to its computational acceleration,
this proposed algorithm has considerable potential for the simulation of complex two-phase
porous media models, such as dense, diverse media.

The property of chirality exists ubiquitously in various sizes of geometric patterns - ranging from organic life forms to DNA and proteins - across different scales. Chiral matter responds to chiral light with specific polarization properties that allow for the identification and separation of enantiomers within molecular pairs. Developing an optical cavity capable of efficiently interacting with one chiral form of a molecule while rejecting its opposite form is a highly sought-after application in various fields. We successfully designed and created a chiral optical cavity that only supports modes with specific polarization properties, ignoring the opposing modes. Resonant interaction between this cavity and the correct handedness of light induces the formation of a chiral standing wave with uniform chirality properties, but interactions with the opposing handedness of light have no effects on this resonance. Moreover, only emitters with matching handedness effectively couple with the chiral eigenmode, resulting in more selective light-matter interactions and enabling novel approaches in studies of chirality in matter and the chiral nature of electromagnetic fields in vacuum conditions.

This paper examines the connection between Jackiw-Teitelboim gravity on anti de-Sitter spaces and a semi-classical limit of two-dimensional string theory, with c less than 1. We observe that the world-sheet theory of this string theory, comprising a space-like Liouville CFT and a time-like non-rational CFT, exhibits actions and partition functions matching those of the JT gravity model. This match, significantly influenced by boundary terms, extends to annulus amplitudes. We also derive the boundary Schwarzian theory from the Liouville CFT and further establish an equivalence in the 1/2-shifted SYK theory limit between the time-like CFT and the JT gravity model.

A spacetime distortion, or warp bubble, generated by the Alcubierre metric can enable massive objects to achieve global speeds faster than light. This research extends our previous solutions by applying the Einstein equations to the warped spacetime. Due to the break of shift symmetry, new non-zero energy components emerge, leading to a complex, highly nonlinear field. However, in vacuum conditions, the Einstein equations are balanced, causing the warp field to self-sustaining. Furthermore, particles, or radiative sources, embedded within the warp field would experience an artificial force, affecting the metric's center.

As urban cities' aging underground infrastructure systems require growing upkeep, cities are faced with the challenge of coordinating maintenance, predicting and resolving issues, and fulfilling their goal of becoming smart cities due to limited understanding of their infrastructure's current state. Most cities lack accurate digital data on their underground systems (electricity, water, natural gas), hindering construction project planning. To overcome these issues, a new framework called GUIDES has been introduced to manage and process data for underground infrastructure systems. This enables a wide range of users - administrators, workers, and the general public - to make data-driven decisions by accessing integrated and digitized information. This demo paper outlines GUIDES' architecture and highlights its core components: (i) the creation of underground infrastructure maps and (ii) the fusion of various types of geospatial data.

To analyze the center-of-mass motion of hundreds of $^9$Be$^+$ ions, arranged in a two-dimensional Wigner crystal, we utilized the interaction between optical dipoles and the ions' spin, enabling the characterization of their transverse movement. This was done by comparing the experimentally measured effects on spin dephasing with theoretical predictions, resulting in accurate estimations of temperature levels consistent with previously documented standards, including both laser cooling constraints and earlier research methods. Additionally, our approach enabled the differentiation between the ions' initial motion states as either thermal or coherent, providing crucial insight. This analysis technique was also used to measure, for the first time, the environmental influence on the ions' movement in a specific type of Penning trap. This experiment's findings set an upper bound on the rate at which individual ions are heated due to electrical noise originating from the trap's electrode surfaces, yielding a value of approximately 5 ions per second at 795 kHz for our particular setup.

TERS is an essential technique for analyzing surfaces with subnanometer resolution. Yet, accurately simulating specific TERS spectra is computationally difficult. Our innovative method combines the primary factors driving the enhancement of the Raman signal – the electromagnetic and electrostatic responses – into a unified framework. The proposed approach incorporates two separate contributions to the Raman signal: one governed by light scattering near the tip's apex, and another influenced by the tip's electric field. Our approach was applied to two distinct scenarios: the interaction of light with a clean silver surface and the simulation of an iron adatom on an iridium (111) surface, which was then verified against actual experimental findings. The results show that the iron adatom's electrostatic response has a significant impact on the local Raman signal, even surpassing the primary electromagnetic response.

We used the 64-m Sardinia Radio Telescope to study the emission of nearby spiral galaxies in the K band. Our goal was to detect the Anomalous Microwave Emission (AME) produced by spinning dust grains in the galaxies NGC 3627, NGC 4254, NGC 4736, and NGC 5055, with particular attention to how their emission relates to the thermal and synchrotron radiation present. To find the dust emission we were looking for, we compared the spectra of the galaxies with a best-fit model using data from radio, IR, and optical frequencies. Although our data revealed a slight excess of radiation at around 20-60 GHz above the predictions of thermal and synchrotron models, the present data did not allow for a definitive estimation of the amplitude of the spinning dust emission power. Future observations with deeper IR and better frequency coverage would be necessary to determine the AME intensity in these galaxies and how it relates to the number of rotating dust grains it contains.

Ammonium sulfate's seemingly uncomplicated nature belies a significant ferroelectric phase transition accompanied by an exceptionally large entropy variation and both electrocaloric and barocaloric properties. For decades, researchers have disputed the underlying cause of the significant entropy change, but this issue is now resolved using a comprehensive approach that incorporates density functional theory-based phonon calculations, inelastic neutron scattering, and additional neutron scattering experiments. In contrast to the previously assumed, albeit widely adopted model of entropy involving disorder of ammonium ions, the current analysis reveals that the significant entropy change originates from the softening of ammonium ion modes and the adjacent As$(N H_4)_4^2$ layers, where the ion's vibrational frequencies drop below thermal motion of the ions at all temperatures, enabling a phase transition. Moreover, it is demonstrated that these systems display not only ferroelectric but also barocaloric and electrocaloric properties with large coefficient values of $-9.5$, $-12.5$, and $-16.5 \,kB/K$ respectively.

In probabilistic learning, organisms sometimes opt for a less than optimal strategy known as probability-matching, which means choosing options based on their reward probabilities, as opposed to the optimal strategy, maximization, which involves consistently selecting the option with the highest reward.  Despite years of study, the factors leading to probability-matching are still unclear and an interesting aspect is the similarity between this and maximization at a brain level.  We provide evidence that explains probability-matching in a simple way by suggesting it is a consequence of an internal learning process called convergent learning.  This process, tested in algorithms and a neural circuit model, results in similar patterns of activity to those observed in probability-matching.  Furthermore, our findings also shed light on the relationship between probability-matching and maximization, which we were able to replicate in our neural circuit model.  Essentially, all-learning outcomes can be explained as variations of the same underlying process, which means different learning patterns may simply be results of the same dispositions in different orders.

A proposed Witting configuration, with a different complexity of 40 rays, could reformulate the Penrose model for spin-3/2 systems based on a dodecahedron's geometry, to study quantum mechanics' nonlocality and contextuality. An alternative setup using 120 states is examined in this work. Despite their different sizes, both arrangements are linked to a common 8D lattice with 240 fundamental vectors, tied to the E8 Lie algebra. An exploration of this setup's properties employs forms of reasoning, including reasoning by analogy and reasoning by imagination. Comparisons with other quantum systems' degrees of freedom are also made in the discussion section.

The continuous Fréchet distance c-approximate near neighbor problem involves precomputing a data structure that efficiently finds closest polygonal curves within a certain radius from query curves, considering an approximation factor c. This problem has been investigated in various contexts, with initial focus on the l2 metric, corresponding to c = 1. For real-time applications, constructing such a data structure for approximate nearest neighbor searches is crucial. Recent progress has been made, particularly in the field of practical solutions. This research aims to provide an in-depth review of practical solutions to the problem, emphasizing improvements over time. We also explore the challenging theoretical side of the problem, which has received less attention in the literature. Despite the different problem definitions and focus areas, a core set of techniques has evolved to address the issue. We seek to highlight the diverse approaches developed to tackle the problem, as well as potential future research avenues.

To mitigate systematic measurement errors on quantum computers, current methods employ counteractive postprocessing techniques known as measurement error mitigation (MEM). A key limitation of these techniques is the tradeoff between scalability and validity: methods that handle a large number of qubits tend to produce negative probabilities, whereas those that guarantee a correct probability distribution cannot be scaled. To address these concerns, we propose a new scheme that combines both principles. Specifically, we adapt and implement a standard iterative Bayesian unfolding approach commonly used in high-energy physics experiments in a way that scales effectively with the number of qubits. Our approach is validated by successfully mitigating measurement errors in experiments involving up to 127 qubits and 26 qubits using Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger and Bernstein-Vazirani algorithms, respectively.

When humans operate robot arms, it is frequently necessary for the robot to infer the task the human is attempting to accomplish. Current research on assistive teleoperation and shared control focuses on developing methods for the robot to determine the desired task based on human joystick inputs. Typically, this is done by using an internal map that links joystick inputs to specific tasks: for instance, pointing versus grasping. One major issue with existing approaches is that they do not inform the human how the robot interprets their controls, making it challenging for the human to understand why certain tasks were chosen or what would happen if the human's inputs confliced with previously selected tasks. In order to address this, our research proposes a new method in which the robot not only identifies the initial task but also clearly explains its decision-making process. We achieve this goal through a graph-based model called 'Task Interactions' which outlines the connections between input commands and tasks, along with various algorithms to predict the initial task and to generate explanations by identifying paths from the initial input to the chosen task. Experiments on existing datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in explaining robot decision-making, while both qualitative and quantitative analysis confirms that users prefer explanations that accurately reflect the initial input they provided.

For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, having an effective mapping system is crucial. Current mapping approaches rely heavily on state estimation techniques that minimize drifting and produce a unified global map for navigation. Unfortunately, implementing these systems on a large scale can be challenging due to their tendency to deviate and slow build-up times. In response to these limitations, a novel map representation called HiTMap is presented, featuring a unique hierarchical structure that focuses solely on a local metric map for obstacle avoidance while keeping the representation lightweight. Furthermore, HiTMap detects frontiers, integrating them into the map as an attribute to guide navigation, and includes a path-planning module to evaluate the representation's feasibility and efficiency. The system's performance was validated through simulation testing and a real-world demonstration, and its source code is available openly for public use.

Research into two-dimensional arrays with favorable two-dimensional correlation properties has gained significant interest due to the rapid advancements in modern wireless communication technologies. Various applications of two-dimensional arrays can be found in areas such as ultra-wide band, 2-D synchronization, and phased array antennas. This paper presents a novel method to directly construct two-dimensional zero-complementary array codes by utilizing multivariable functions. Based on this novel approach, two-dimensional ZCA code construction is performed using a multivariable polynomial, and the parameters of the resulting code are determined. To validate the novel construction method, an example is employed to generate a two-dimensional ZCA code with the length of 201x201 and a low 2D correlation magnitude of around 0.03 and a correlation peak to the maximum value.

Computed Tomography (CT) is extensively utilized in both engineering and medical fields for creating detailed images of internal structures within various subjects and objects. Since most X-ray sources emit X-rays of multiple energy levels, which vary in their absorption rates, the process of reconstructing images typically involves a reverse ray transformation process. Omitting these variations may result in image distortions such as beam hardening, which poses an additional challenge. In certain settings, the dual effects of radiation and electronic signal degradation caused by devices such as CCD cameras contribute to image degradation. A proposed variational reconstruction model effectively accounts for these two distinct types of noise as well as the polyenergetic X-ray source, and further distinguishes between materials with unique attenuation characteristics. In support of this model, a related algorithm is presented, analyzed, and applied to synthetic data, with comparisons drawn between its results and actual scanned data produced using CT technology.

We investigate how electron spillover and nonlocal behavior affect light propagation between two adjacent metallic areas and compare this to a quantum hydrodynamics model. We demonstrate that a quantum hydrodynamics model which incorporates both phenomena yields accurate results, particularly as the gap narrows, in contrast to a local response model which generates unappealing results such as divergent fields and excessive light scattering. Notably, the amount of spillover and short wavelength cutoff needed to be considered are much smaller for very small gaps, but still require consideration far beyond what can be detected, thereby indicating very short emission zones.

In this research, we investigate the connection between human identification of context-sensitive words and the process of natural language documentation. We present two studies where participants manually select terms that are significant in their own projects, revealing both common and distinctive context-sensitive words across these initiatives. We compare the effectiveness of both automated and human-identified context-sensitive words in retrieving relevant information from documentation, using two evaluation metrics that consider accuracy and overall retrieval strategy. We found that although some automated methods can resemble human choices to some extent, ultimately, manually selecting context-sensitive words leads to better search outcomes. We discuss the implications of our findings on current practice, suggestions for enhanced documentation tools, and possible future investigations in the field of documentation.

Time-based data refers to information measured against time, giving us a clear sequence of past present and future observations. Most real-world data we have exhibits temporal patterns - for instance, the price of stocks tends to trend higher during strong economic periods. When analyzing data over time, we often see repeating patterns such as seasonal fluctuations, frequent patterns and trends that change slowly. While working with time series data poses challenges, leveraging time-based information can greatly enhance our ability to identify trends, prevent costly mistakes and gain a better understanding of the underlying dynamics of a given problem. In multivariate time series analysis, we study how individual data streams relate to one another - this is particularly important given that individual data feeds often contain subtle yet important connections. In this reading, we'll explore the fundamentals of processing multivariate time series data to understand how various data feeds relate to one another. We'll cover the basics of visualizing relationships between different data feeds, comparing the characteristics of different data feeds and techniques for analyzing the direction of influence between them.

The promising potential of extracting valuable insights from Electronic Health Records (EHRs) has emerged as a crucial area of study in the medical community, as it can significantly contribute to enhancing healthcare quality by facilitating individualized care. However, the challenges associated with the complexity and heterogeneity of EHRs data stand as a major obstacle in the field's progress. Despite the advancements made by expert clinicians in identifying abnormalities and correlating them with relevant medical literature, the process remains prone to inaccuracies and confined by individual expertise. In recent years, the integration of Machine Learning (ML) in EHRs has gained momentum, as it seeks to aid clinicians by complementing clinical knowledge and augmenting diagnostic capabilities. A particularly effective approach in medical applications involves the utilization of Knowledge Graph Embedding (GIE) techniques to create dense representations of EHRs data, as they possess inherent semantic information and can facilitate meaningful learning outcomes. Our research aims to bridge the gap between patient care and technology by focusing on a new patient-centric task known as 'identifying aspects of concern', as influenced by patient age and comorbidities, in the context of EHRs data. To achieve this goal, we developed CAKE, a system based on GIE, which enables the production of informative representations from patient records and enables 'aspect-based' concern identification. Our approach is distinguished by its use of 'contrastive learning', as it enhances model robustness by comparing similar patient records, as well as 'position-encoding

Using a mean-field approach and considering both non-uniform particle sizes and solvent effects, we model the behavior of the electric double layer at the boundary of a charged flexible material. From a free energy model, we calculate the electrostatic potential and number of water and ions within the boundary using coupled differential equations, including the Poisson equation. We discover that solvent effects profoundly impact the electrostatic potential, ion counts, and permittivity of the electrolyte near the boundary of the charged flexible material. Furthermore, we find that taking solvent effects into account intensifies the Donnan potential and demonstrates that within the boundary of the charged flexible material, the ion counts are higher than in a solvent-free model, while the counts outside the boundary are lower. Additionally, we find that the electrostatic potential exhibits a greater absolute value than in a solvent-free model both inside and outside the boundary.

Automating the labor-intensive and error-prone process of extracting requirements from unstructured text is a major advantage, as it enables organizations to make informed decisions faster. Advanced natural language techniques are now applied to requirement artifacts to generate requirements summaries efficiently. However, researchers often overlook how project-specific language norms influence overall performance. While general language models can achieve decent outcomes, they fall short when dealing with unique terminology and context unique to each project. In light of these disparities, we re-evaluate the performance of pre-trained models on requirement extraction tasks and introduce a novel approach that leverages project-specific data for improved text-to-text performance. Our research showcases the effectiveness of leveraging project-specific data for requirement extraction using fully unsupervised training methods, showcasing superior TF-IDF or rule-based methods performance on three publicly available datasets without extensive training. Moreover, our models exhibit improved stability and better performance when faced with new, previously unseen requirements.

This research investigates the energy efficiency in a multi-user, multi-relay communication system with a maximum diversity network coding technique. A direct link between outage probability, energy consumption, and energy efficiency is established, followed by a formulation of the optimization problem to maximize energy efficiency under the constraint of maintaining a target outage probability. A practical scheduling and power allocation strategy is implemented to minimize power usage. Since the optimization problem is complex and difficult to solve, a tight approximation is first used to simplify the outage probability, then energy efficiency is re-expressed in a different form and the optimization problem is re-cast into a solvable form as a mixed-integer non-linear problem. A generalized outer approximation algorithm is then applied to find a solution that simultaneously optimizes scheduling and power allocation, showing how to obtain the best possible energy efficiency gains by optimizing these two strategies. A comparison with a no network coding scheme is conducted to validate the efficiency of the proposed strategy, and numerical results demonstrate its effectiveness in achieving the desired outcomes.

A comprehensive theoretical framework is developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model focuses on YSR states born from the hybridization of local spins and paired conduction electrons. As a result, distinct spectral features emerge consisting of resonance peaks, gap edges, and deep hole-like states. To track down these elusive YSR states experimentally, we discuss suitable methods like impact autoconvolution and subtraction of bulk spectra, that could potentially make these phenomena observable in real-life experiments.

Techniques such as the Normal Distributions Transform (NDT) can efficiently register and accurately bound point cloud errors for scenes without dynamic changes.  However, traditional methods struggle in scenes with movement like traffic or leaves blowing in the wind.  To address this limitation, we developed a registration and error bound computation tool capable of handling changing scenes.  This tool employs a dynamic point cloud filter to establish correspondence between distributions and then computes error bounds by the Hausdorff distance.  The proposed method was tested on point clouds derived from an aerial laser scanner and compared with the NDT method, showing improved performance in scenes with dynamic elements.  The tool and associated code can be accessed at https://github.com/lieu-d/distributed_registration.

Satellite images are widely employed across multiple sectors, encompassing 
agriculture, urban planning, disaster management, and defense, often necessitating
manual annotation for specific objectives like land use mapping or object detection. 
The availability of large-scale image datasets has grown, yet corresponding ground
truth data can be difficult or costly to obtain, leading to the adoption of
semi-supervised techniques where annotated data is scarce, though fully automated
options are often preferred when possible. This paper focuses on the efficiency of
two semi-supervised and fully supervised models on two datasets: 1) a small
agricultural dataset with limited labels, and 2) a construction damage classification
dataset with annotated specimens drawn from the National Damage Survey.

Subjecting solid materials to an ultra-intense, femtosecond X-ray pulse from a free-electron laser causes drastic electronic excitation, triggering swift changes within the material's electronic system that unfold over the duration of the pulse. The amount of X-rays absorbed by the material becomes contingent upon the energy flux, giving rise to a unique form of X-ray absorption near edge spectroscopy. Researchers can study valence excitation on the few-femtosecond timescale with this type of XANES spectroscopy, allowing for in-depth examination of electronic dynamics near the edge's energy peak. Recent studies on both nickel oxide and multilayered graphene, carried out under varying X-ray fluences, have revealed distinct changes according to the material and the XANES technique employed. Notably, flavor-dependent fluctuations were observed in studies involving nickel oxide, while the studies on graphene showed fluence-dependent shifts in the delocalized π orbitals of the material. The findings from these studies suggest that ultra-intense XANES spectroscopy offers a novel approach for investigating the rapid evolution of excited electrons in strong-field interactions.

The application of a Deep Neural Network in Automatic Modulation Classification (AMC) exhibits enhanced performance compared to traditional methods even in harsh wireless environments, but this can be compromised by targeted adversarial attacks that inject noise into wireless channels. This paper presents a new method based on a generative adversarial network (GAN) aimed at protecting AMC from such attacks, using label noise to train the network to reduce errors caused by small perturbations in the input signals. The proposed mechanism combines two approaches: a generative model creating noise that mimics the adversarial attack, and a discriminative model identifying and rectifying classification errors caused by the attack. The method has been tested using the RML2016.04 dataset and the results show that it effectively increases the robustness of the AMC system against perturbations in various scenarios.

Segmentation of Multiple Sclerosis lesions in MRI scans is a difficult task due to variations in appearance and labeling. Previous approaches relying on deep learning have segmented lesions by matching image patches with pre-labeled examples, often resulting in incorrect or incomplete segmentation due to limited training data and poor generalization. We developed a deep learning method that learns and adapts to local patterns within the MRI scan without relying on pre-labeled data, and calculates a "lesion score" to guide segmentation and fill gaps. When tested using a specific model and training dataset for lesions in central white matter, the proposed approach successfully identified 88% of lesions in an independent scan, outperforming compared methods.

A novel type of metric comparison analogous to Alexandrov comparison is established, 
and its relationship to optimal transport between measures on a Riemannian manifold 
is demonstrated, specifically with respect to the MTW condition proposed by Xi-Nan 
Ma, Neil Trudinger and Xu-Jia Wang, involving a notion of continuity.

Across various disciplines, there's considerable interest in creating predictive models for complex systems using data, and in particular, there's ongoing research in continuous-time systems, which aren't influenced by the discrete time intervals used to collect data. Earlier research developed techniques to construct data-driven models for specific systems, but a recent paper has created a general approach applicable to a broad range of systems, including those with linear, nonlinear patterns, and even those that don't follow predictable lines. The new approach is based on a specific mathematical expression, called a differential equation, which can be created using both linear and quadratic terms. The research found a connection between the length of time intervals, general error rates, and other factors. The results were verified for specific systems, and a recent discussion included examples of systems that don't adhere to predictable lines, as well as potential future areas for further research.

A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, specifically protostellar and starless cores.  Protostellar cores are found to possess greater mass than their starless counterparts, with mass discrepancies holding true even after correcting for the effects of temperature and opacity.  We interpret this observed mass difference as a sign of mass growth among cores, with far-reaching implications for the origin of massive star formation.  In essence, it challenges the conventional view that massive star formation must originate from massive prestellar cores.  Further research is necessary to thoroughly explore this finding's effect on the established relationship between the mass function of prestellar cores and the mass function of their protostellar counterparts.

The theoretical primordial black holes that may have formed in the early universe are proposed as a possible type of dark matter. If these black holes exist, they can potentially be identified through specific astronomical phenomena. The text examines the interaction between extreme cosmic events and black holes in various stages of their formation. The discussion focuses on how the collapse of massive overdensities into PBHs might occur, as well as how the distribution of these overdenships could impact observations of specific astronomical events. The investigation also considers early black hole mergers and expulsions, which could leave behind remnants with properties similar to those of neutron star mergers. The potential for detecting these residual black holes is complicated by incomplete understanding of early cosmic conditions, but researchers can use current knowledge to set upper bounds for PBH formation based on key events such as gravitational wave observations. The potential for future detection of cosmic events influenced by PBHs is also explored, involving deep space observations of specific astronomical phenomena.

We conducted research into systems of monodisperse wedge-shaped molecules through computer simulations, exploring a wide range of conditions including varying temperatures, pressures, and chemical potentials. Analysis revealed multiple liquid crystalline phases, including bcc and plastic crystal phases at low packing densities, and smectic and nematic phases at higher densities. Notably, we discovered a unique plastic crystal phase with maximum molecular arrangements and high lateral fluidity. Furthermore, we found complex and unconventional mesophases, including a phase without long-range order in one dimension, and another phase combining nematic properties with distinct molecular arrangements. A comprehensive theoretical framework was developed to understand the phase behavior of these systems.

Our goal with parameter-efficient tuning is to minimize updates to model parameters
when adapting a pre-trained model to downstream tasks. This paper proposes PASTA,
where we adjust only the special token embeddings, like separator and classification tokens in BERT, just before self-attention operations in each Transformer layer within the model. By doing this, PASTA can achieve performance on par with fine-tuning for natural language understanding tasks such as text categorization and named entity recognition while updating a mere 0.029% of all parameters. Furthermore, the flexibility of PASTA allows for its effective application across various pre-trained models like BERT, ALBERT, and XL-BERT, as well as being extendable to hidden states within the model, resulting in even better performance outcomes.

This paper investigates a complex problem where we need to assess the impact of adding items to a collection. The inherent nature of this problem prevents us from making absolute preferences between options, which prompts the use of context-dependent preference modeling. To tackle this issue, we examine two distinct Siamese network designs, contrasting one that compares the resultant collections after an addition with another that considers each item's individual contribution to the existing collection. Through experiments involving a real-world task of learning Magic: The Gathering deck-building card preferences, we found the former network more effective. Alongside the inherent complexity of this task, we identified several crucial factors that contribute to the performance variability of the used preference modeling approach.

Our application of the lattice cluster theory for polymer fluids has established that the configurational entropy, enthalpy, and internal energy are interconnected thermodynamic properties as supported by recent experimental data from Caruthers and Medvedev. This relationship enables us to reframe the generalized entropy theory for glass formation, combining the lattice cluster theory and Adam-Gibbs model, based on any of these properties to simplify the analysis. Additionally, our previous findings concerning entropy and energy correlations, especially the significance of pentamers and hexamers, remain valid even in this revised framework.

Transformer-based language models have been shown to struggle with logical reasoning, especially when it involves negation. Unlike previous studies that relied on psycholinguistic tools, our research delves into types of negation from developmental psychology. We examine this knowledge gap through a natural language inference task by creating a set of specialized questions from existing NLI datasets, which helps us assess a range of models' ability to process these negation types. Our analysis indicates models perform notably well on some negation categories, revealing a significant distinction in their handling of this concept.

In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, raising the question of whether existing attention models effectively model this dependency. We propose the UVAttention model, where UVAttentionKernel is a customizable, analytically computable function that can be applied as a layer or pointwise operation to enhance various attention models, thereby reflecting target word dependency. We model target word embedding as a comprehensive representation of all possible target words given the partial generated sentence, viewed as a high-dimensional combinatorial space. We also propose a target word re-ordering mechanism to minimize unnecessary computations in UVAttentionKernel computations. We evaluate UVAttention on six translation tasks and achieve better results while reducing computational complexity, outperforming existing models consistently.

This passage provides an in-depth, explicit calculation for the weights of Kontsevich graphs that emerge when examining Kontsevich graphs associated with symplectic manifolds of curvature, specifically focusing on graphs involving one hole. It also outlines connections to the weighted Chern-Simons theory and to the recently introduced symplectic curvature technique.

This research involves determining the vacuum entanglement entropy in various spacetimes 
proportional to $S^{d-2}$ in dimensions $d$ from 3 to 9, using the $O(N)$ CFT method. 
By adopting an unconventional approach that first evaluates the CFT method's defined 
operators at large $N$ rather than $O(N)$, we demonstrate a straightforward calculation 
for entanglement entropy across all levels, discovering a universal wavenumber-independent 
entropy in the given spacetime and dimension, $d \geq 3$. Furthermore, we calculate 
the entropy's logarithmic coefficient in dimension $d = 3$ and finds a relation between 
these coefficients for different dimensions $d$. In higher dimensions $d = 5, 6, 8, 9$, 
we determine the wavenumber-dependent entropy's behavior.

Cai, Song and Kou made a significant contribution in 2015 with the development of a universal approach for pricing Asian options based on one-dimensional Markov processes. This note applies the CTMC framework, calculating the inverse Z-transform and inverse Laplace transform separately for discretely and continuously monitored options. As a result, we achieve improved explicit Laplace transforms, surpassing a prior theorem by Cai et al. and yielding increased efficiency through numerical studies.

The source behind the diffuse gamma-ray background is currently unknown. However, various galactic features such as star-forming and starburst galaxies, black holes, and cosmic clusters may all play a part in this phenomenon. Researchers conducted a study that simulated how cosmic rays interact within galactic clusters using cosmological magnetohydrodynamical models. Their analysis, spanning a range of redshift values, suggests that clusters of galaxies could account for up to 100 percent of the gamma-ray flux measured by Fermi-LAT at energy levels above 100 GeV, assuming certain conditions are met. Specifically, these conditions include specific spectral indices and energy cutoffs, and clusters of a certain mass and redshift. Their predictions also anticipate future observations of high-energy gamma-rays from clusters using upcoming experiments like HAWC and CTA.

A straightforward cosmic model has an inflationary phase driven by a massive scalar field and a single rolling quadratic potential field. The calculation of perturbations shows that during inflation, the phase of oscillation aligns with the potential's anti-node, yielding a more significant correlation between the Fourier modes of the cosmic curvature fluctuations and the quadratic potential coefficients at the time of oscillation start. Consequently, the power spectrum of the cosmic curvature fluctuations exhibits an enhancement proportional to the high-frequency wavenumbers and decreases proportionally to the square of the ratio of the oscillation frequency to the Hubble parameter, specifically when the oscillation frequency is twice the inflation rate. This model's properties are such that a more significant deviation from the uniformity of the Fourier modes results in a negative non-Gaussian parameter, denoted as $f_{\non-Gaussian}$.

Understanding how complex visual models work is crucial, and developing techniques to explain these models can be particularly challenging. To address this issue, a framework called LaViSE is proposed to enable convolutional neural networks to describe their internal workings in plain text. By using generic image data, this approach creates a link between visual and semantic information, allowing for its application across different domains without explicit labels. The LaViSE framework has a flexible structure, making it possible to analyze any network, regardless of whether its training data is accessible. Moreover, this technique can produce new explanations that go beyond the categories initially learned during training. It also has a significant application in discovering biases within datasets without needing additional labels. To facilitate further research, the framework, datasets, and code are openly available.

Developing a simplified microscopic model of cuprates is crucial in uncovering the mechanism behind high-temperature superconductivity in these materials. Many models ignore the interaction between electrons and phonons in cuprate molecules, assuming this coupling is weak. Contrary to this notion, our research indicates that long-range electron-phonon coupling significantly influences the interaction between electrons within cuprate materials. We demonstrate this coupling can lead to a strong attraction between adjacent electrons, a phenomenon unaffected by the presence of holes. We further investigate the structural features within cuprate materials and demonstrate how the interaction between electrons and phonons affects the empty upper Cu 3d band, thereby creating bound pairs of electrons. We show that near the critical temperature for superconductivity, the resulting attraction between electrons is enhanced, enabling the formation of a density wave that transitions into a superconducting wave at a slightly higher temperature. Our results indicate that superconductivity in cuprates results from the coexistence and competition between these two types of ordering phenomena.

The ongoing Population-based HIV Impact Assessment project aims to measure national and regional progress in combating the HIV epidemic, a primary goal of UNAIDS' 90-90-90 targets. By analyzing data from high-risk countries in sub-Saharan Africa, researchers hope to gain a deeper understanding of the key factors driving the epidemic. As a result, countries can develop more effective strategies to control the spread of HIV. The project's success relies on the accurate estimation of HIV prevalence and associated 90-90-90 metrics through a robust and efficient approach that incorporates sensitive reporting mechanisms. Drawing from the experiences of previous surveys that employed multiple data collection methods, researchers have developed a approach to merge data from different sources, including face-to-face interviews and through-line facilities. The results show that the estimated population sizes of different groups, such as men who have sex with men and sex workers, are unique to each country, though they differ significantly from the assumed values in the model. Furthermore, researchers have identified key factors associated with the awareness of HIV, including age and education levels, while highlighting the challenges posed by the lack of reliable data on at-risk populations, ultimately threatening the achievement of the 90-90-90 targets.

In the chiral magnet Co$_9$Zn$_9$Mn$_2$ of $\beta$-Mn type, researchers discovered a stable "topological skyrmion lattice" over an extensive range of temperatures and external magnetic fields, despite the presence of competing phases. Utilizing microscopic magnetization measurements, scientists found that this phase is characterized by uniform interlinked skyrmions with consistent size and the same directional orientation. Notably, the area occupied by the skyrmions is directly proportional to the applied magnetic field strength, achieving the predicted ideal condition known as the "N\'eel order parameter". What differentiates this material is its ability to maintain this phase over a broad temperature profile, ranging from room temperature down to 5K, thus making Co$_9$Zn$_9$Mn$_2$ a prominent candidate for applied quantum research.

High-Dimensional Dynamic Factor Models are thoroughly explored, covering key 
assumptions and their underlying rationales, significant outcomes, and example
exhibits through simple demonstrations. The theory and implementation of 
these models, focusing specifically on singular ARMA models, is examined. The 
paper prioritizes detailing model types and their underlying structure, 
rather than estimation methodologies, aiming to highlight innovative 
research avenues and applicable areas which are still underdeveloped.

The equilibrium problem described by the Nikaid\^o-Isoda-Fan inequality encompasses several key problems like optimization, variational inequality, and others, as specific instances. This paper aims to provide a clear outline illustrating the connection between fixed points of the Moreau proximal mapping and solutions to the equilibrium problem that satisfy particular monotonicity and Lipschitz-type constraints.

Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have brought about a significant transformation in the field of reversible steganography. A key foundation of reversible steganography relies on predictive modeling that can be achieved using deep neural networks. However, critical inaccuracies persist when dealing with data outside the scope of a model's training dataset. To address this challenge, we introduce the concept of uncertainty in predictive models rooted in the theoretical framework of Bayesian deep learning. Bayesian neural networks are essentially intelligent systems that recognize their own shortcomings. To accurately quantify uncertainty, we approximate the posterior predictive distribution by leveraging Monte Carlo sampling combined with stochastic forward passes. Furthermore, we demonstrate that predictive uncertainty can be separated into aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties, both of which can be learned through unsupervised methods. Experimental findings show that the application of Bayesian uncertainty analysis leads to greater success in reversible steganography.

The debate on turbulent effects influencing magnetic activity in the Sun and stars persists. The mean-field theory provides a widely applied framework to link these effects to fundamental magnetohydrodynamics, although it's not possible to observe these effects directly. To gain insight, researchers utilize global convective dynamo simulations to explore turbulent effects, which are measured by their impact on energy transfer and angular momentum transport. In a study focusing on turbulent effects in the solar tachocline, researchers used the Pencil Code for convective dynamo simulations to investigate turbulent effects in a region where rotation supports stable stratification. According to early findings, energy and angular momentum are primarily transferred via turbulent motions near the tachocline interface. Characteristic lengths and time-scales associated with these effects were determined using structure factor analysis. As a result, energy transfer was found to be influenced by a specific function representing the energy spectrum, whereas angular momentum transport was linked to the inverse momentum spectrum. Further investigations involved adjusting key parameters, such as rotation rates and specific properties defining turbulent effects, to identify their impact on stellar magnetic activity. The study identified topological small-scale circulation as a critical mechanism influencing turbulent effects, which were found to be significantly affected by rotation rates, though not thermal properties. According to the research, energy and angular momentum transport are primarily achieved through mergers and splits of convective structures in the momentum transport scenario. Conversely, when considering energy transport, these effects were found to be primarily achieved through turbulent motions. The study

A study has revealed strong, highly localized blobs of molecular gas within the central area of the galaxy NGC4945. These gas plumes, visible in the form of absorption, have been identified through high-resolution VLT CRIRES+MIDI spectroscopy. The plumes' speeds match those of previously observed ionized outflows, both in terms of speed and spatial distribution. The fastest plume detected had an estimated velocity of approximately 246 km/s and was observed in association with a region of intense HII regions, hydrogen recombination, and gas outflows. The data suggest that the gas outflows are driven by Ejecta fragments interacting with the gas outflows for the first time, resulting in the formation of these plums observed in the velocity field of the gas outflows. The gas outflows have been observed to press against the gas disk of the galaxy, causing the gas outflows to move at the speed of the gas outflows rather than the speed of rotation of the galaxy, thus indicating that the gas outflows are having a backflow effect on the gas in the galaxy, this backflow effect is preventing the gas outflows from going beyond a certain speed. A simplified version of the original gyrokinetic equation for magnetized plasmas is derived using an exact method based on a specific expansion, providing a new insight into the interaction between particles and waves in these plasmas at different scales. The fully expanded version of the gyrokinetic equation precisely describes the resonant interaction between particles and waves, resulting in a simplified form that captures the main characteristics of this interaction at large scales, while ignoring other non-resonant effects at smaller scales. Although this simplified form seems to discard wave-particle resonance, we demonstrate that such resonant interaction can be consistently recovered by describing the gyrocenter motion within a bounded region rather than at a specific point. By applying this approach, we recover the locally-conserved energy and Poynting flux, in addition to the conservation of particle number and momentum. The novel formulation of the gyrocenter equation we present here has the potential to significantly improve the numerical solution of gyrokinetic simulations for turbulent plasma dynamics.

Previous variable stepsize Second Derivative General Linear Methods, achieved direct strong stability by utilizing a single equation involving the second derivatives, where the original formulation was only applicable to fixed stepsize methods. Researchers have developed a new second derivative general linear method that maintains strong stability at each step, utilizing two equations involving second derivatives, along with an expression that can be evaluated at both the current and previous steps. An efficient implementation of this new method has been developed using non-standard finite difference formulas. Researchers have constructed such formulas that maintain strong stability, have high order accuracy, and can be taken to a conditional order of convergence, all properties inherent to SGLMs. The resulting new method has been shown to possess several desirable properties including strong stability, high order accuracy, and conditional convergence properties, all under certain conditions of its coefficient matrix. The study also confirms its previous formulation as being weakly consistent, further establishing its current formulation as being strongly consistent. Furthermore, researchers have performed an in-depth analysis of its important properties, including order, strong stability, strong consistency, and convergence, using certain conditions on its predictor. Specifically, they have looked at the behavior of the method when its predictor is consistently of a certain order, along with other conditions not related to the predictor. The study also includes a formal characterization of its conditional convergence properties, where it remains an open question whether the method actually converges conditionally.
